div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

A BIT in the morning is better than nothing all day. "A MAN never loses anything by politeness2'- How about his seat in a street car? THE man. Who does not believe that two lieads —itiaibetter than one is the father of new tains. WHY ism ripe currant as a tree like Home Buie?, —Because there you have a current topic (curnint to pick). WHEN a man has to Chalk his head and use 41 shoe-horn to get his hat on, it is time for him to think seriously of reform. SOCIETY is just like a pie. There is an upper crust and a lower crust, but the real strength and substance lies between them. REPORTER—" Is there much maney to be anade out of opera ?" Operatic Manager—" A good deal more out ot it than in it, I should judge from my experience." THE following was overheard in the Pork the other day. He—" I hate walking out without an object" She—" Oh !as to that, I heldot r. go out without my husband." TOT was receiviag his first lesson in geography. "What is that?" salts the professor, placing his finger upon the ma. "That," answers Tot, "is a dirty finger-nail." "A SEAMAN washed overboard," exclaimed Mrs. Fangle as she read a newspaper headline; "but he perhaps was so dirty they hadn't enough water on the ship." WOMEN are liable to make mistakes, but not one of them, at least no white woman ever gets so far wrong that she puts pulverised charcoal on her face instead of pearl powder. COUNTRYMAN (pointing to the -obelisk)—" and what's that?" Citizen—" That's Cleopatra's needle." Countryman—" Needle, gee ram 1" Citizen—" Yes, she used that to sew her wild oats 1" HUGO ARNDT, himself a Jacobite, used to say . of a certain Jacobite physician, who flourished in Edinburgh half a •century ago, that he had slain more of his own party in a professional way than the sword and gallows united. BARRISTER, in renlyigg to his antagonist in Court, aid he had a keen rapier with which to pierce all fools and knaves.; whereupon his opponent • moved the Court" that the rapier be taken from him, lest he should commit suicide. sCHOOLMASTER recently informed an anxious mother that her sons were so thoroughly disciplined that they were as quiet and orderly as the very chairs in the schoolroom. It was probably becomes they were cane-bottomed. PATIENT--" Oh, doctor, you don't know how ik worries me to think that I might be buried alive 1" Doctor—" Calm youreelf, Mrs B. You need have no fear of anything like that Trust to we, and I assure you that you are in no danger." Miss Eritzi.—" Ido so admire Mr. Rierso's figure. : He has a fine figure. He has a very fine presence. What do you think of his carriage, Mr. de Garmo ?" ' Mr. de Garmo--‘‘ Well, really, -Miss Ethel, Idea t know as Lever saw him out driving." "No," said the yrouth," I don't intend keeping a regular diary. I only want a book to set down my daily thoughts." "Ah ,I understand!" replied the intelligent shopkeeper. "Then, of course, you wants smaller book than this." INDIGNANT mother—" Tommy, you IMISHI Sit down to the table with your cap on." Tommy— " Now, ma, I'm a member of this family, and I don't see why I'm not entitled to the same privilege as grandma." 'Did ye have a good time at the election last night?" "Indade, I did." "Was there any fun?" "Very little—that is, what you would call fun." "Did you make any motions? "Jist wan; but the brick slipped out of me hand intirely, and the President called me to order wid his club." "Sours," said the schoolmaster, "is what you hear. For instance, you cannot feel a sound." "Oh, yes, you can 1" said a smart boy. "John Wilkins," retorted the pedagogue, "how do you make that out? What sound can you feel ?" A sound thrashing," quickly replied the smart boy. Two New Yorkers alighted from a street car at the Grand Central the other day, and one said to the other—" By Jove, that was a beautiful girl who got in last, wasn't she ?" "Yes ; she's a stranger in the city." "How do you know?" "She said Thank you' to the man who gave her his seat." A NIINISTER at a coloured-wedding, who wished to be humorous, said—" On such occasions it is customary to kiss the bride, but in this case we will omit it." To which malignant remark the ?room pertinently remarked—" On such occasions it is customary to pay the minister 5:2, but in this case we will omit it. NEVER change your politics, my son. It is bad enough to have the opposite party showing up your Past career. When your old political associates begin to advertise you their 111f1.11£1 of information are so superior to those enjoyed by your enemies that the result is disastrous. No, my son, never change sides. "SIR," said a Yorkshire publictu to a man notorious for never speaking the truth, "you have taken away my character." "How so?" said the other. " I never in my life mentioned your name." "No matter for that,' rejoined Bonifo.ce ; "before you came here I was reckoned the greatest liar in the place." ELDERLY GENTIIMAN (who has been talking to a young fellow from Philadelphia, and has taken a great fancy to him)—" By the way, where are you staying? I wish you woald come and visit me." Young Fellow (who is a friend of elderly gentleman's son)—" Why, lam staying at your house. I have been there a week." linown—" lye got an excellent plan for getting rid of duns." Green—" Ha! that's so?" B. —" I have; never fails." G.—" Then, old fellew, you must let me into the secret, for I'm worried to death by 'em." B. —" Well, I've tried it several times of late, and I rind the man never comes back again." G.—" Ay, ay, what do you do ?" B.—" I pay him." AN old Scotch worthy who had lost his case in a Court of Justine was asked by his wife, when he got home, how he had got on. "I've lost," said he, "but I gie'd the shirra up his tit." "Bit, Tammas," she asked, "cud be no punish ye for that?" " I tarn guid care e' that," said Tammaa, "for I was six miles ,ay road harne afore I

opened my mooth." SIIE—" Mr. Brown, will you give me a trifle toward our African mission fund ?' " He—" Why, certainly ! Here is ten dollars I won at whist last night." She (horrified)—" Oh, dear, no. I could not touch that. He—" Well, here's ten dollars I made on the Stock Exchange to-day." She (pocketing the cash)—" Oh, you are too kind. I am ever so much obliged." A LADY wrote to a clever authoress to beg her to procure a tutor for her son, one endowed with every imaginable qualification of mind and heart. Her friend replied, "My dear N., lam lookingior a tutor such as you have described; but I have not as yet been happy enough to meet him. I shall continue my search with unabated zeal, and I pro- mise you that as soon as I have found him I will— marry him I" IN the execution of a recent deed by a man and his wife, the wife was taken aside, before the acknowledgmeut was made, by a commissioner, who, in the usual form, asked, "Do you execute this deed freely, and without fear or compulsion of your husband ?" "Fear of my husband !" ex- claimed the wife. "I've had five husbands, and never was afraid of any one of them." ,6 You attend Sunday school, do you ?" inquired the Rev. Mr Smith of Nellie. "Then you must know a great deal about the Bible, Now, tell us something nice that's in the Bible here, can you ?" " Yetis. thin Sic bath some dried leaves in it, a pieth of Aunt Jene,'s weddin' dreth, a pieth of my dreth when I weth a b•-4by, thome haie, and Sis' fellow's picture.' "DID I pay for that wine we had last night, landlord ?" asked Crirnaon coming down one morning with his heed tied up in a towel. " Why, you ought to know, Mr Critissenbeek," replied a bystander, jokingly. " Well," maid Criineoebeak, " I consulted my pocket-book. and it accused to • nay that I did ; but when I consulted my head I came to the conclusion that I was paying for it this rnornieg." " THERE," said Mrs Highfiyer, as her daughter ceased from torturing one of the high-numbered ," ops." of Beethoven. "that's what I call a finiehed performance, ch, :11. Jones ?" And Me Jones nodded and sahi, " Th.tbk Heaven."

Colonel Wauchope'3 poll le understood to have represented ths high 'water inark ot ecclesiastical influence, while •neghgence and over confidenos had re- duced the numbers on the winning side. We are glad- te note that General Booth confirms and •emphasises his offer to submit the accounts connected with the special expenditure on the " submerged temtli " to a committee of enquiry. We agree with him that as to the composition of the.committeeit should be easy " to secure the co- , operadon of those who command the confidence of all rightnininded men." A correspondent of the " Times " suggests that the .expenses of registration should not reet, solely on the - shoulders of Parliamentary canuidates. The public should, he thinks, contri- bwe a.share. ,Of course they should. The cost of registration,onght to be defrayed from the public puree. The ,question arises opportunely at a moment vs-ben we cannot too often or too strongly ineist upon the obligation which is laid upon all 'wlio have the vote to see that their names are 'Awed upon the register. " The "spectator," referring, in an article upon Yewspopers and the Church," to the courtesy of " masters of theological as of other fence," says : Itis usually reserved for less distinguished corn- batents to give the rein to their tongue from the moment they begin to write." " Combatents," " rein;" " tongue," " write,"—really, Mr. "Specta- tor," this is an alarming mixture of metaphors. It reminds us of the theolegian—we do not know whether he was a " master of theological fence"— who told his congregation that he was " happy to see that the. Gospel-trumpet, which Paul planted and Apollos watered, is bearing such good fruit in your midst. a

The Rev. Mr. Haweis's ladies' surpliced choir is not such a new departure tv London people seem to think. The idea first originated with the late Dr. Bromley, Dean of Melbourne, who introduced lady choirsters into the Pro-Cathedral in the white sur- plice and mortar-board cap. This was fully tire years ago, and created such a sensation at the time that Di. Bromley's choir ran Sydney Herber close as one of the sights best worth seeing at the Antipodes. The men marched up the church first, and when their fair assistants followed, wear- ing their college caps, strangers in the congrega- tion usually ..got a shock, supposing that the choir rear-guard were irreverently keeping their heads covered in the sacred edifice.

The " epigram " to which the " St. James's Gazette" gave prominence on Tuesday on the sub- ject of the Derry election, is not so novel or original as our contemporary seems to suppose. It is really a variant on an old Irish election rhyme. For in- stance, on the return of Sir Charles Gavan Duffy for New Ross in 1855, it assumed this form :
" A year or two since Igave a great shout, When I heard that our friend Gavan Duffy was out ; I haven't changed since, not the point of a pin, But I'm twice as glad now to find that he's in."

The " out " tl'e second line is a refence to Sir Gavan's release from prison after Dublin Castle had brought him to trial three times for his connection with the abortive rebellion of '4B, and had on each occasion failed to secure a conviction.

The Duke of Richmond, who on Monday received a large party ot almost annual guests at his fine seat, Goodwood Park, for tile Goodwood Races, is a short, stout, red-faced man with bushy whiskers. He is a very good business man, and has worked hard both in the Lords and on the Sussex County Council. He is not a brilliant orator, but he can " talk "very much to the point. He is a great authority on railway rates, and keeps his game- book 08 regularly as if he were a ticket-clerk and the birds were colored squares of cardboard. It is a curious fact that though be is not fond of racing he is the owner of a racecourse and the father of one of the principal racing lights (the Earl of March) ot the day. lie suffers from gout, and goes to Hom- burg almost every year to take waters in order to obtain temporary relief.

There was a remarkable scene at the English Opera House on Saturday evening, at the end ot Sarah Bernhardt's farewell performance. Of course the great actress was again and again the recipient of enthusiastic plaudits. But when the curtain had fallen, and Madame Bernhardt had several times been called before it loud demands were made fot "Dumont," the brilliant young actor who played the part of Searfpin in " LaTosca." Instead of Darmont, however, Mdme. Bernhardt again ap- peared, bowing and smiling, and gracefulty waving her arms.. This went on for some time until the audience got angry, as the actress, and not the actor came on the stage. The lights were lowered, but .this did not restrain the ardor of Darmont's ad- mirers, and at last, when there was nothing else for it, the tragedian appeared. Then one heard the most uncomplimentary remarks regarding the great Sarah's transcendent egotism.

The question of the right of the public to fish in the River Trent is just now occupying, the atten- tion of the Retford county police magistrates, and much legal and historical learning has been ex- pended upon this subject. It is admitted that if the Trent comes within the legal definition of a tidal river, then the man who by way of a test case has been summoned for taking eels in its waters at Rampton was within his right, unless the Crown had in ancient times granted a charter to the con- trary. But what is a tidal river? The prosecu- tion contend that a river is not tidal at any point where the waters are not brackish—a doctrine which would prove that the Thames is not tidal anywhere between Greenwich and Teddington Lock. The Trent at Rampton, it seems, regularly rises and falls twice in the twenty-four hours, and the difference has been known to amount to six or !ieven feet; but in the view of the prosecution this IS not the first effect of the tides. As one witness i I put t, "There is a little backing-up of the river," but he" did not call it a tide." The magistrates have taken time to consider the judgment.

"Tokin' mates," said Billy, the cut carrier, "aw yerd a comical Buie touch th' other Uay abeuvrt an Irishman at Wigan an' hiv mate.' . . . .

" 0, aye," said Snoaree, rousing himself with an effort, " rive hi o, awn wakken.-' " It's a wonder," said Billy ; " thaell be, asleep ageeon afoor aw'vederne. Aw wonder iv thee ever gees to bed. ileawever, this young Irishman lived at Wigan, as ow wer sayin'; an lied olsz bin a tabourer up tie a format sin'. Last week but one, heawever, th' gaffers at one o' th' coyl pitslell short hands' at th' pit, an' to mek th' number up they took Pat ate another young fella on as" drawera'— aw think that's wod they co 'em. Pat an' th' other , -mon started off together th' fost morniti"at they'd: to go to th' pit.; but in abeavvt an heawr a•cousin o' mine 'at lives o'er theer met Pirt•comin' backhooam lookin' as" sackless ' as iv be wer off to a funeral." " Hallo., Vat;" said mi friend, 4‘ what's to -do as thae'rt cconin'back °ready; be ta nod getten on at th' pit?' "0, yis," -said Pat, " oi got on, right enough." "Well, dud th' wark nod suit tha, or some'at?" "0, shunt, it was worrse than that," said Pat, "the work was varry fair; but ye see, oi'd hardly got stitarted noicely afoor mi mate tumbled roight down the pit, an' oi came away at wance." "Whey, tha dudn'd need to come away" "A:h, but thin," said Pat,"how could you expect me to go on workan without mi mate! ,Oi‘couldn't shtand the thing, at all, to work without tai mate." An' wi' that Pat toddled off beawt sayin' another word; an' mi friend went his own rooad. Ile bed to pass th' coyl pit on his way.; so he said he thowt he'd cons he wer gooin' 114 y, an' ax o'er Of accident so long as Pat lied bin r to' big a horry,to give him ony information. So he-dud-col an' questioned th'

feat • chap he coom across. "Sad job this," he said " hey theytgetten him iap yet" "Wod ?" said th' chap. 44 Hey they getteu him up yet?" .4;Letten whooa U yet?" " Whey, th' core, to be sure--thad young fella as tumbled deawn."

" Whey, whooa the th' chap axed. "Thad young fella 'at coom wi* Tat Flanigan," said'ml friend,—" aw dornd know his name." "Thae'rt ayther a foo,or somebry's bin tryin' to ,rnek tha one," said th' chap.; there's nobrg :tumbled deawn here:"

" Well," said mi friend, " this is a rich bit o' puddin', heaw 'c be. Aw met Pat deawn you, an' axed him wod he war gocin' hooam for, an' he said because his mate hed tumbled deawn th' pit, an' he 'couldn't work tart him?' _

"Mate, mate?' th' other "chap said, as he scrat his beead, "who is his mate—o,aw.know,—Tim O'Hara. He's yon. Here, Tim, tome here:!" Tim coom, an' wer towd as Vat hed bin settin' id oawt 'at he'd tumbled &awn th' pit. " Oi'll never that ov um," said Tim, " anyhow." " Well thae'rt his mate, are'nt tn.?'" said th' chap. " His mate, is it? "said Tim, an' his e'en twinkled 6' a sudden. "Ah,bigorra, now O'im one ov urn; but it's his other mate he'd be meanin'. An' Tim Carted laugin' like a cleawnsan' med O' ring ageeon Wl' his din.
Wod mate, Oa gaumleas meawntebank ? " mi friend axed.
His mate that he atee " ' Tim sbeawted, "ye two balf-witted sinners. His breakfast an' dinner fell

down the pit ;an' id was such t mess when we got it up agin that he couldn't ate it. Oi'd aten moine an' had none to give urn, so he wint shtrate home to get another slitock. That's all4gi know abeawt L'at's mate."
An' n 1 wer quite enough for th' other two.—From the Freston Guardian.

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT A PINCH 0' SNUFF! Neaw, Bob, eawt wi' thad box 6' thine,-- Aw'll hey a smell wi' thee; Tha'rt one o' t' gradely upreet sooar Aw'm allus fain to see. Tha proves thisel' as true as steel, W ben'e'er tha'rt put to th' test ; So sit thee deawn, hey a sooap stingo--th' varra best. When Nature meke sich chaps as thee, Hoo's nowt but sterlin' stuff -; Sit deawn, mon, then aw'll dib, tek A friendly pinch o' snuff. Mi nooase is seldom ticklish, Bob, Unless tha'rt bi mi side; Then th heawrs go rattlin' on, an' Time 0 deawnbroo seems to glide. We dorn'd meet oft, but when we do, Ther's comfort i' ml' heart. For aw con crack a jooak, an' know Tha teks id i' good part. A bit o' bullock suits thee wee!, Tha ne'er dies in a "huff," But smiles, when sumbry meks a hit, An teks a pinch o' stuff. • Thar't pictur ov a true John Bull, A hearty Englishmen; Wod " buzzes" o'er th' dow-days tha's towd, An' th' family porritch pon ! But yet, i' o' thi ups an' deawns, When th' " times wur eawt o' joint," Tha ne'er geet deawn to th' Floghton fare— Cowd " buttermilk and' point I" Now, nowe ! The owd cock who towd thad tale Wur hearty, blunt an' tough ; He laff, then axed us if we'd hey A gradely pinch o' snuff! • Hey, Bob ! wod happy heawrs aw've spent Wl' t'other mates an' thee; Wod gam flaithed reawnd, while every fare Wur breet wi' rooasy glee. For when we geet together, we'd Enjoy pawrsels someheaw, Wi' recitation, song an' jest, An' th' bite' " Thuston's ceaw." We've getten scattered neaw a bit— Fate's used some rayther rough— But dorn'd think we'st forget to co An' ged—a pinch o' snuff! Wod " gentle deeds" that's quately doue, An' thowt no eyes cud see ; Ther written deawn th' Book aboon ; Some's locked i' memory. Aw wish thee fortune, health, an' strength, An' happiness, owd lad ; An' th' same to o thi kith an' kin ; May yo'r hearts ne'er be sad; But if misfortune threatens yo' Wl' some unkind rebuff May every trouble disappear Just like—a pinch o' snuff 1
JACK O. ANN'S.

div.head: TRAMCAR INCIDENT.
div.p: A TRAMCAR INCIDENT.

A pretty girl, faultlessly attired from the top of her bonnet to the tips of her dainty patent leather shoes, jumped on a tramcar in a great hurry. She had been busily engaged in putting on a pair of long suede gloves, which, after she entered the car, she proceeded to button with that indispensable adjunct to a women's toilet, a hairpin. This article proved refractory after a moment, and flew from her fingers. It landed at the feet of the young man who happened to be sitting beside her. Ile was a calm eyed, confident young gentleman, and he picked up the hairpin ; and, instead, of returning it to her, gently took her wrist in his left handand gravely continued the buttoning process. Every man in the car had been watching the pretty girl some openly, others furtively, from behind their newspapers. Now all the papers dropped, every- one looked aghast, and gazed at the pretty girl to see what she would do. She did nothing. Not a muscle moved, and she showed no consciousness of what was going on. The young man with a con- scious look of triumph, finished his pleasant task, and the girl, with a preoccupied air, and not a glance in his direction, opened her purse, took out a coin, placed it in his hand and left the car.

BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN.
).I..telkor of" Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Wnere the North Wind Blows," dec., dec. _ • _ _ .
CHAPTER LIX.

AN OMINOUS SOUND. All was quiet in Breamish Hall, after the whirl 'of hurry and excitement had subsided; and Madam ' was left alone there to meditate over the events which had happened and were still happening.. She felt strangely restless, and could not settle to any occupation. What would this visit of Lance's to Seaton Callerley bring about? Not a reconciliation. She scarcely even wished for that. If they would be kind to the boy—that was all she could now venture to hope. Even that she had no right to expect, 'and—if they did but know— But they never would 'know. Only one person besides herself was cognizant of the crime she had committed; and for the sake of the living, the secret of the dead would be kept for ever. But no assurance of safety could prevent hor- rible dreams or hinder them from coming to Madam. Even the previous night, when the burden had fallen from her spirit for a while, and her heart was eased and comforted by her boy's caresses, it was not of Lance she had dreamt when tardy sleep came to her at,last. It was another child clung to her bosom then; tiny infant for which she had not love, and one that wailed and cried incessantly, and refused to be stilled, even though, desperate with anger, she placed her hand over its mouth and Merciful Heavens! How tenaciously it clung to her breast, and how strangely heavy it grew. Its soft flabby lingers were like unto the suckers of some creature formed by nature to hold fast upon the surface I of rocks. Every now and again she made an en- ! deavour to throw it from her, but the effort was always futile. It was too persistent, and it seemed to get stronger and stronger every minute, as though .it absorbed her vitality, and left her too exhausted to cope with it. Instead of being able to get rid of it, it dragged her down instead; down, down, always down to where yearned s great gulf, a fearsome gulf of darkness and dread. Even when wide awake once more she could see that dark gulf, by simply closing her eyes—the im- pression of it was so strong. There was something else that troubled and caused her the keenest regret; and this was the simple fact that Lance, in the hurry of departure, had left without giving her a kiss. A hundred times before had the same thing happened without causing her the slightest feeling of uneasiness, but this morning it seemed an unbearable thing that no farewell greeting should have passed between them. Aimlessly the mother wandered into her boy's room, seeking for comfort and finding none. The bed was just as.he had left it, for as yet the ser- vants had not begun to set his room in order. The impress of his little figure was still upon it, and the woman threw herself down and laid her guilty head where the innocent one of her child had lain. No peace came to the restless heart from the sense of contact. The lack of a childish voice, of quick, pattering, impatient feet, of shrill, boyish laughter, struck -A chill upon her fancy. The rain beating against the window panes in- creased the sense of discomfort. How dreary and desolate it sounded. The war of the elements out- side—solemn stillness within. Impatient of her own feelings, Dorothy Breamish rose and looked out of the window. It was a day of sudden storms and watery gleams. The storm had complete mastery at that moment. What a day for the boy to be out in! • She was • sorry now that she had allowed him to go. She wondered how far he had got upon the • journey. Perhaps no further than the Widdrington's cottage? They might be sheltering there until the storm was past. What caused her to be so anxious and wretched? There was no danger threatening Lance. Sir Lancelot, her kinsman, would take great care of that ; however muck he might hate the mother, he would certainly guard the child. Hark! Whence came that sudden gust that rushed through the house, shaking the doors and the windows with fierce vehemence, and dying away in a sad wailing sound? She held her breath and listened. Something coming, or to coma:, some strong yet indefinite terror seized upon her, and seemed to stop the very beating of her heart, to intensify and absorb all her faculties into the solitary act of listening.

Listening for what? One moment there was not the slightest sound perceptible. A stillness as of death reigned within the place. The very wind had' crept away, and the rain had ceased to patter .against the window pane. Then suddenly, as by magic, the whole air was filled with a soft, beating continuous noise, a noise as of innumerable pinions. The room appeared to become the centre of some great fright of winged creatures, whose downy pinions pulsated and vibrated throughout the whole .of the enclosed space. Dorothy Breamith gave.a gasping, sobbing sigh, and walked feebly to the bed. With a gesture, like that of some cretlture stuck to the heart and blind with supreme agony, she felt about there in the spot where her boy had lain. Her eyes, dazed and wandering, looked wildly around,. as though they could not take in the fact of his absence. Then quite suddenly she burst into a'loud and =- earthy laugh. "My bonny boy," she 'cried in a hoarse, broken voice, he has proved a Callerley after all! My blood—my blood has been too strong in his veins—it has brought his death—his death von him 1"

When the servants entered the room some time after, they found her lying without sense or motion, and so ghastly and pinched were her features that they fancied her dead. But alas, it was her brain, not her body, that succumbed to the shock. Death I did not come to her—only madness. The madness which had been stealing over her subtle schem- ing intellect for the past year had triumphed now. Her insanity took d singular form, but luckily for those about her, not a dangerous one. Each infant she kV, r>he took to be her own boy Lance, gone back to leibyhood. When the mothers of these babies declined to give them up to her, she would weep bitterly, and refuse to be consoled. . ' &length a happy idea was conceived by the woman who attended upon her. This was to pro- cure a big doll, and dressing it in the clothes of in- fa.ney; give it to her, to nurse and fondle, instead of those children she could not have. This plan answered admirably: It was a strange Sight to witness the grey haired woman (for Madam's hair had turned grey after that dreadful hour) nursing and cuddling and ,crooninei to that clamsv wooden doll, lavishing upon it more caresses than ever she had giver, to ,her own child. , * •• • • •

"I will come and meet you, Lancelot," said Lady Callerley, going with her husband to the door of the hall, and looking out over the landscape, see, the sun is shining brightly now, and I shall ;Tot too dull for anYtlling without; you." "You might have ridden with me, had you spoken sooner, dear, answered Sir Lancelot, though to he sure I, have tclio on to Breamish before I return, and may be detained there some time.. And then ;Hawkins says, 4ritomart. is sliFhtl7 lame V' , Yes, she got a stone in ' her shoe yesterday; 'ptioll dear, it haa cu' her foot.. Nevermind I ;have had no exorcise lately, and would. ,greatly prefer to walk I You will probably- &I'd me at the IYraclringtons' cottage. I am anxious" to see; the little lad, as soon as possible!' : . "All very, well, but am I to ride home, and leave you to walk back alone." "I am going to bring Bell back with me, BO I shall not be alone," replied Lady Callerley quickly, " Ailsie is going te' be there tnr-day, fk. Bell can leave her grandmother for an hour or two. It will , be a change for her, and I want to hear all about r her approaching wedding. There is no chance of a talk about it while old Nanny is listening. She says such things." The baronet smiled. " Every detail of a love affair interests you, Silvia," he said, "You never tire of the subject of wcodm •gs.l, "When one is so happy' oneself, one would fain have the rest of the World so, Dear Lancelot, how did I live before you loved me 5" As she looked up at him, her young face all aglow with happiness, and her voice tremulous with emotion, a sadden pang smote him, a sense of pitiful tenderness.' He felt almo4 sorrowful because of the intensity of her love. He was so greatly her senior that he had scarcely a right to fill her life so that nothing else should signify! _
*ON

CHAPTER LX. A WORLD OF DESOLATION. In ordinary seasons the Yarrop was little more than a simple hill burn; but it drained a large space of country, coming from the high-lying moor- land to westward; and in seasons of heavy and continuous rains it gathered and swelled into a con- siderable river. _

Such a season had this last autumn proved, and Yarrop burn was a powerful torrent in conse- quence. When the tide.was in, it overspread the great level stretches of sand by the sea shore. At all times these Callerley sands were treacherous, but at these and kindred times they were doubly so; and the fisher-folk avoided them carefully, taking wide circuits rather than venture upon crossing them. Upon the receding ,of the tide the burn rushed swiftly and tumultuously down to the sea; and Bell could hear it shaking the wooden piles of the bridge, as though it were engaged in a wrestling bout with them.

-- ----- With each fresh downfall of rain the stream rose visibly. Every new accession of waters sent before it a threatening crest. If it rained much longer the bridge must inevit- ably go. Nevertheless there were intervals of cold and brilliant sunshine, during which the world appeared like unto a bride adorned with pearls. One of these intervals took place upon the morning when Sir Lancelot, in accordance with Lady Callerley's wishes, rode to the Widdringtons' cottage in order to bring back little Lance Breamisli to be their guest at Seaton Callerley. Lady Callerley, following on foot, had herself reached the cottage' and after resting there for a while and making Lance's heart dance by her tender reception of him, had set out upon the homeward path, accompanied by Bell Widdring- ton. The boy did not go with them. He was to stay at the cottage, and there await Sir Lancelot's return from Breamish. Silvia thought him look- ing white and tired, and judged that the walk from the hall had been too much for him without further exertion. After proceeding a little way from the cottage, and glancing back, Lady Callerley was rather startled to perceive the figure of old Nanny stand- ing in the doorway, and apparently watching them closely with her glittering eyes. "Why Bell, there is your grandmother; she has come to the door to watch our departure. I scarce thought she could have managed to leave her chair, and to travel so far without assistance."

The fisher-girl herself appeared to feel surprise. "No more did aw," she replied quickly, "she's gotten some queer notions in her head, ye may lay yer life on't, or she wadn't ha' left her warm seat i' the chimney corner. Daft and wife! Whatever's come to her, te make her gan on 'i sic a fond fashion '!"

Simultaneously the pedestrian stood still, and gazed at the strange antics of the old woman. They were descending the bank towards the bridge, and this was why her figure—small in reality—seemed to stand out towering and dig- nified against the sky. She was holding her hand to her ear as though , to assist her in listening intently to the sound of the rushing Yarrop, and as she listened an expres- sion of horror grew into her face. All at once she clasped her hands and lifted them on high in an agony of appeal; then, as though to shut out some dreadful sight, threw her apron over her face, and tottered back into the house.

.-udy-C-allerieTranduelir looked at each other in bewilderment. What was the meaning of this strange piece of by play. At length Silvia, who was just then in too gay a mood to take anything seriously, burst out laughing. Did you ever see anything so utterly wild and incomprehensible? Why Bell, child, I really believe she was calling down a curse upon you for. .running away and laving her with Alike to- day." , But Bell had no answering smile. ,For once the common sense was on the lady's side, and the imagination upon that of the fisher lass. i " Aw'd as lief she'd kept i' the chimney corner," ehe said, in slow and hesitating accent. "It wasn't canny, you listening to the Yarrop ater. She often foretells queer things which she positively declares are whispered to her in that way. As for me, aw'd as lief she'd bidden where we left her l"

," Whatever the water has said, al least it could ,bein no whisper, but in a roar such all the world might hear," was Silvia's comment, as the two drew near the raging torrent. "Listen Bell! You cannot call that a whisper." , They stood hearkening in an awestruck way to the stormy music, and then suddenly Bell ran on before and crossed the bridge. Her reason for thus stealing precedence of Lady Callerley was a kindly one. An unconquerable doubt of the stability of the wooden bridge possessed her. She therefore determined upon being the first to test its powers of endurance. , She decided that these were indeed small, even though both Lady Callerley and she crossed in safety. Bell's own fine well-developed figure caused the structure to shake and to sway .in a very perilous fashion, although Lady Callerley's lighter weight passed over with little more than a slight quiver- ing vibration, not very alarming. "Is Sir Lancelot coming this way ?" asked Bell rather anxiously, lingering by the stream. "Why yes, child. It is ,mile round to go by the other road. You do not think there is any danger "'kebbe. there is. Aw never fancied this wooden bridge inysel'." Nonsense Bell. Don't you copy your grand- mother, and imagine that every evil under the still .aust needs happen because you have had bad dreams. It appeared steady enough when I crossed t.

Tohat is a very different matter. 'Vera nowt .; ut efeather's weight., Whon it dt0Ille:? to a full grown 'nail on horsehipli}inl a boy forhye.that'll .try the rotten timbers if Sjelike." The girl ,was so', evidently in •carnest in her fears for Sir Lamsdot's safety, that she managed to ini- ipresii -Lady Callerley with some slight-measure of !drean also. . "We had better Wait ,Iscre the,-if you think it ; to risky. By that means we can warn Lancelot not to make the attempt Aftinecall; there is something in the look of • the wates 41ittt -I do' not quite Row it goes curl*. writhing round the piles, as though snaking Sly and continu- ous efforts to uproot them." The pedestrians upon coming to this resolution sat down under the shelter of .a high 3:.}sulbasili. ; Here they were sheltered in some degree from the wind, and caught and basked in the watery gleams of sunshine. Lady Callerley spread upon the sand A shawl which she carried, and so they were pretty snug and comfortable in their lowly tasting place. Lady Callerley began to talk of Bell's love affair, and insisted upon hearing the girl's avowal of her entire contentment therewith. "When 1 and happy I'imust needs tell everyone about it," said Silvia, half piqued at the reserve of the fisher lass, "But you North-country people— there is no understanding you. You seem ashamed to confess any great affection,' seem to think it a crime to love too welL" Bell's eye kindled and her cheeks glowed. "Dick knows. Ma canny Sweetheart knows. Aw dinna see it matters to any other body, if only him and me understand one another." "yes, yes, of course. And what Of Cuddy? Is he going to follow your example, and to wed the many childed widow." "Aw fancy not. He disna' gan there as much nowadays. He's ower particular, is wor Cuddy. Folks should all be made efter one pattern to please him... I,le.eatched her in, a bad temper one day. She wasg.tirinr young Mat his licks for not e_attin' off hi # BiNg history' Cuddy took the lad's _

>7 , 'l{. SATURDAY, '',II.ILY 30 ;1892 yii.J y "dearest," he said with grave TH "I sometimes t' \ilk that I have been E CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS. ' extreme to hint., )our young existence to one which must inevitably, by the laws of nature, end ere yours has reached its prime? But men are selfish, and love is selfish, whatever the poets may say. I have at least loved you, Silvia, with all my heart. Never forget that, dearest wife." "Husband ! I know that you have loved me with all your heart," replied Lady Callerley, rais- ing her head proudly, and gazing back at him, her blue eyes full of infinite devotion and tender- ness. "Is that knowledge not sufficient to >fill my life for evermore? Love is eternal, and life and death are mere episodes in its existence. Talk not to me of selfishness ! We arc one, not two.; so how can there be any selfishness between us.? I have lived to some purpose, since I have lived to be your wife. One hour of perfect love is better than a lifetime of doubt and of indifference. Kiss me, Lancelot, dear, and do not talk such nonsense unless you mean to a,nger me 1"

_tic upshot W 21.4 that they came to high wen-, on the subject, an' she told Cuddy that he was a- backslider, an' was on the fair way to damn- ation." _ _

"What an awful woman. He is exceedingly wise to withdraw in time. Dear me. How cold and dark it has suddenly become. I wish we were further on our road, and that my -husband would come quickly." It was indeed too true that the weather had changed for the worse. The sky darkened ominously above them, and a vast and overwhelming cloud had settled over the western horizon. From a Sigh, faint and softly sweet, the sound of the wind had risen to a moaning and despair- ing wail. Quickly the tempest broke overhead. In vast and drenching sheets the rain descended. There was no possibility of flying to a better place of shelter. All they could do was to crouch still lower in their hole, burrowing into the sandhill after the manner of rabbits. They were the prisoners of a phenomenal storm. "Oh, Bell, how dreadful this is," murmured Lady Callerley, crouching nearer to the fisher girl for warmth and for .a sense of. companionship, "what will Lancelot do'? I do hope they have not started yet, because if so they may perhaps wait until the storm is over."

There was good reason for alarm. Rushing down from the high moorlands, the rains swelled the Yarrop with astonishing rapidity. Great mountains of witer seemed to rise as by nm.foc, and come tearing down from the hills. Through the blinding rain, Silvia at length dimly discerned the form of a man on horseback approaching the stream. "He has not waited," she cried, wild with excite- ment. " Oh Bell, whatever shall we do? I fear that our voices will not carry so far through all this noise and tumult." _ .

Sir Lancelot was evidently in no mood to loiter, for he was urging his horse to its utmost speed. They could now see him more distinctly, and see also that the boy Lance was there behind him, clinging around his waist. Above the tumult they could also hear the beating of the horse's hoofs, pounding the muddy road. In a minute or two the bridge would be reached, and it would be too late to atop him. Lady Callerley glanced at the Yarrop water, anc'. the sight filled her with overwhelming dread. The torrent seemed at least to have doubled it- self. Besides this, from the distance a foaming crest was tearing down toward the bridge. It was difficult to say which would be first to reach the spot, the rider on horseback or the huge mountain of water. The race was pretty even so far. Sir Lancelot still kept urging on his horse, evidently not at all realising his danger. Silvia ran out from her shelter, and waved her arms' frantically shouting at the same time to warn him; but instead of answering the purpose, this served instead to quicken his movements, and render him all the more eager to join her on the further side, He would not understand that she meant to warn not to beckon; and the sight of the little figure awaiting ,him diverted his eyes from the threatening crest of wave. When lie at length glanced up, instead of down the stream it was already too late to retrace their way. About the middle of the bridge it would be equally perilous to turn as to continue. With a quick grasp of the situation he did the only thing possible; that is he dug his spurs into his horse, and the noble creature answered the challenge by an eager bound forward. The effort it made proved, however, to be futile. The race was indeed won and the goal reached, but alas, not by the horse ! A vast and overpowering volume of water struck the bridge. Not merely did the crazy structure sway or break in two under the ponder- ous onslaught. It was carried away bodily. Right into the midst of the angry and boiling torrent were horse and its riders at once pre- cipitated. When this event took place, a shriek rose up from the spot where Lady Callerley stood helpless, watching the frightful scene. It was quite evident that even in the midst of his deadly peril this shriek penetrated to Sir Lancelot's ears, for he, recovering from the first shock of his fall, shouted to reassure her : "Silvia, fear nothing ! I will fight for my life !" _ _

Through the wild uproar the words readied her ear; and she held out, as in answer, arms yearning to enfold him safely. Sir Lancelot had somehow contrived to retain his seat., and still did the boy cling to him. Strong horse and strong rider were alike power- less against stronger torrent. Yet did the gallant. beast manage to keep him- self afloat, mad with fear as he was; and half swimming, half battling for dear life, and help- less against the tremendous propelling force of the great mountain of water, all three were carried downwards toward the sea. _ _

The water was often up to the chins of those who rode Despair; and occasionally it rose higher; but still they clung to their seats. One feeble ground of hope alone remained to them. The tide was an incoming one, and consequently it was in some degree stemming and arresting the flow of the torrent near to the mouth of the burn. When they arrived at the wide estuary of the Yarrop it might therefore be just possible to so direct the horse as to escape the , sweeping cur- rent. If it were possible once to gain a footing on the sands, the fearful danger would be past. Sir Ts,ncelot Callerley, who was not for giving up the fight without a struggle, calculated upon this— their last and desperate chance. Calm and re- solved, he awaited the opportunity, eye and hand alike ready. It came to pass exactly as he had hoped.. Where the stream overspread the wide range of level sand, it grew at once more shallow and less boisterous.

Amid stream were some low rocks; and the horse, guided by Sir Lancelot, managed to gain a temporary footing upon these. The poor brute was snorting and panting with its tremendous exertions, and shaking in every limb. ( Great flakes of foam flecked its wet and shining sides and flew forth from its nostrils. Fear as well as ex- haustion had seized hold upon it. The rocks lay in the midst of the stream, and all around, as far as the eye could reach stretched wide spaces of sand, and shallow pools of water. Sir Lancelot breathed more freely. He put his hand behind him uo feel if the lad were safe, and

was relieved to find that the little fellow still clung there, like limpet to rock. "Can you hold on a little longer, Lance ?" he said, and the lad laughed at the question. He had scarce realised the peril through which they passed.hAd "No fear of me Cousin Lancelot," he cried, with spirit," I shall come to small hurt while you are. in front Of me." Thus assured, Sir Lancelot made him ready and braced up his muscleslor a fresh start. All aglow was he with the excitement of a victory. . : But in the eagerness of the moment he entirely overlooked another danger that lay straight before him. •Once more he put spurs to Despair; and while the creature was yet trembling and feeble, they left the firm rock for the treacherous sands. , Unfortunately these said sands were by this time little better than shifting pools and quicks ; and it was not long ere Sir Lancelot recognised the irre. trievable blunder he had made. The good horse, that had hitherto fought so amazingly for dear life, could here gain no secure foothold, and floundered about upon the quick- sands in a helpless and feeble manner. Lady Callerley stretched out her arms enee more to her husband—her lover. Buf there is no

response. Lord ha' mercy on them. Thoy''ve gotten on the shifting sands 1" exclaimed Bell Widdrington ; and then, with a sudden impulse, she stepped in front of Lady Callerley, and held up her apron so as to Shut out the view of what was taking place. But a great and heartrending cry burst from Silvia, as she rushed, to one side, and 'ran down the bank to the water. "Wait, Lancelot ! Let me die with you," she. screamed in agony, flying blindly onward into the stream. But Bell was almost as quick ill her movements. She, following, put her arms around Lady Cab lerley's slight figure and carried it forcibly to the bank. When she laid it down there, with exceed- ing care and tenderness, she was rat her relieved to find that merciful unconsciousness had come over the bereaved wife. It was some time before Lady Callerley recovered her senses, and rose feebly to her feet. Then, putting aside Bell's protecting arms, she looked around with, Stunned and wistful incredulity. "Lancelot, come back ! Come back, or take me too I" she cried. But the voice that would hays answered her so readily was hushed for ever. On this barren and pitiless shore_ skte_Lvas tp_ 1e alone, until. the dawn
-rf')kllS; part.
of that eternity through which she had said love lasted. Even at this terrible moment her own words

came back to hex. "Love is eternaL Life and death are mere episodes in its existence." God belp her. She had foreshadowed the fate which had overtaken her. Despairingly she gazed around. No trace of the gallant horse or its Adore Was anywhere visible. The place where last her eyes had rested upon them'was now empty of all but mere sand and water. As though in cruel mockery of the tragedy cold sunlight played over this part of the beach. Suddenly as it broke passed the storm away, and pierced the sun through the heavy clouds. The sunlight gleamed upon a great pallid space a sand, and pallid pools of water innumerable. A sense of intense stillness and lack of move- ment was over all. Not even the flash of a ses bird's wing broke the quiet of that world of dew- lation.
THE END.

DEATH OF LORD bfiERBROOKE. ----- The death, on Wednesday, of Lord Sherbrooke- brought to a close the career of a man in whom intellectual gifts of a very high order were quali- fied by defects perhaps chiefly physical. Mr. Robert Lowe, who was the son of an Anglican clergyman, the Rev. Robert Lowe, rector of Bing- ham, in Nottinghamshire, was born at Bingham, December 4, 1811. The "Daily News" says :—By the death of Lora Sherbrooke the number of living ststestnen who. have been Chancellors of the Exchequer has been • reduced to six. During the present reign the office has changed hands no fewer than tweuty times. Mr. Gladstone has been Chanoellor of the Exchequer four times. Other ex-Chancellors of the. Exchequer are Mr. Childers, who was appointed in 1882; Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, 1885; Sir W. Rat- , court, o February, 1886 ; and Lord Randolph . Churchill, who succeeded him in August of that year. The sixth name is that of the present bolder of the office, Mr. Goschen. When the hour of meeting in the House of Loris was altered some years ago, the following lines. appeared in "The Daily News So long as their Lordships assembled at five, They tound they had nothing to keep them alive ; By wasting more time they expect to do more, So determine to meet at a quarter past four. They were published anonymously at the time. But there can be no harm now in saying that the author was Lord Sherbrooke. Mr. Lowe's classical allusions were frequent an 4 felicitous. At the time of the Jingo fever he pro- duced this quatrain, founded upon the familiar of Virgil : Tu regete imperio populos, Romane, memento.. . . .

Pa rce-re su binds, et debeila" re super6os. Mr. Lowe wrote: To govern, men, 0 Roman, was thy care, To crush the mighty, and the weak to spare : But Britain's sons a cheaper glory seek, To spare the mighty, ami to crusn the weak. When Mr. Montague Corry, Lord Beaconstießn:- private secretary, was raised to the Peerage as Uri Rowton, Mr. Lowe is reported to have remarked,. " There is an imperial precedent. Did net Caligula make his horse a Consul ? " Lord Sherbrooke was an Albino, and it was tc this defect in his eyesight, referred to in our memoir, that was due a most painful scene in the House of Commons shortly beim e be became a" peer. Mr. Lowe came down prepared to make a. dashing onslaught on the Ministry of the day, and his speech was looked forward ro with the keenest interest, especially on the Liberal side of the House. The introductory remarks gave promise of . a speech in his most trenchant style ; but he had hardly opened his fire on the Ministers before he was reduced to utter helplessness by the discovery that there was some confusion in his notes, whieh' owing to his difficulty in seeing he could no& rectify. A colleague tried in vain to assist him, and Mr. Lowe himself became 60 mortified and un- nerved by this accident that in the middle of a sen- tence he completely lost himself, and abruptlY sa down. The House was much touched with this painful breakdown of one of its most brilliant debaters.
"THE WEAKNESS OF OUR STRENGTA" linute

Now let us reason together, you and I, for a rn our or so. Does the above phrase—The weakness of strength—seem like nonsense to you ? Well, it is not' nonsense, all the same—by your permission. Let ths

see. There are two kinds of strength in the human bod Y- - strength and vital ttrength. The latter is borne • with us, the former may be picked up or cultivated- Muscular strength enables a man to accompliA great' manual labo_ir ; vital strength gives him long life and high health. That is why it so often happens that women who cannot lift twenty pounds live longer, en- • joy more, stand greater exposure and privation,and bear , greater sorrow an affliction then men who can with, ease lift a barrel of flour to their shoulders. If you have • never noticed this fact you need a pair of strong We- tacles at once. Here we have a man who writes a letter from 147, Fisherron, Musselburg, N. 8., under date of May 28th. 1891, and he briefly tells what happened to him not long ago. He says that up to October, 1888, he wa& very strong and vigorous. At that time he had run a race for a prize, and as he thinks, overstrained the muscles of his lungs. In running, we all knoW, the lungs and heart must work hard and fast, as a locomo- 4 tive at sixty miles an hour must burn a lot of'coal snore than when she goes slow. Well, our friend, Mr. J. H. Jack, whe writes tha letter, was presently seized with intense pain, and went to the Edinburgh Infirmary and was under the care of the doctors there for some time. hut it turned out that the doctors were not able t. help him. They blistered him, rubbed hirn with strong liniments, and gave him;various things t 4) take; but their treatment scientific though it must have been—failed to get at the cause of that pain. A man must climb or fall ; it is naturda law. Being unable to climb, Mr. Jack begenloWl-- fall, as he puts it, " into a low, weak way." He began to have things that are bad for a° athlete ; bad for anybody. He says: " I had bad taste in the moutbi, a poor appetite, and after eating I felt ereat pain in the chest and a Isnr Oat tightness, as if a strong man embrace.d and squeezed me so I could hardly draw breath- `- fact, I suffered so much I couldn't sleep at night' and it was all I could do to attend to my business. This was the kind of life I lived for months, oatil August, 1889." Ilia, al none of all the rnedi6"es I had taken did pne any -good, I made up my Mind t° try the much-talked-of Mother Seigel's Syrup. "I same to do this because I frequently heard custotn- ' crs who came to my sfliop speak of what it had done tor them. It may be hard to behest', but the truth is that after I had used only a single bottle all the pain in snV chest and sides passed away entirely. Then my SPP"I° came back by degrees; I could eat and digest my foods and so gained strength with every dose; and in foie creeks I was cured. By taking an occasional dOse I en- joy excellent health notwithstanding the severe strain which my lungs sustained." Now, what does Mr. Jack's experienco prove? It proves that there was somewhere' an organic weakness in a strong man, which his great exertion to win the foot race developed into active disease. All power collies • from our ability to digest and assimilate food, and from nothing else under the sun; and when In man insists upon having mere physical strength than he has anY real need of, some other part of Lim must soofle:r loss- It was so in this case. The stomach broke' du" and pretty soon the whole body came near breaking down with it. In plain English, Mr. Jack brought ur on himself a sharp attack of indgestion and dyspepsia and all the pangs and pains he had to endure were merely Con- sequences and symptoms of that. One moment more and theiesson is ended. England is a country in which athletic sports of all sorts are more practised than in any other. We may say they are over- done. Young men pile on riuscle, but, when excessive it is always at the expenseo the lungs, heart, and diges- tive organs, the latter especially. Hence we see that it is not to the naturally- weak and feeble alone that Mcther Seigel's Syrup is so great a boons but also to the straig and vigorous, who so often dis- cover to their amazement, how closely allied the muscles are to the food which creates them.

div.head: bfA-lOR PICKMBRPI ON THE OLD AND NEW SCHOOL.
div.p: bfA-lOR PICKMBRPI ON THE OLD AND NEW SCHOOL.

- _ MAJOR PICIMERE then addressed the audience. He said that it had always been the custom hitherto to have some most eloquent man or statesman, or other gentle- man in a high position, to preside on that occasion, and present the prizes. But they had departed from that custom in having on the present occasion a town-bred man to perform the duty. He thought one reason why he had been chosen to preside was that it was 60 years that year since he became a pupil of that grammar school. (Loud applause.) He could not refrain from saying that vast changes had taken place since he became a pupil of that school. When the head master alluded to the death of a dear old gentleman well known in Warrington, Lord Wininarleigh, he admired the feel- ing manner in which he spoke of him as a governor of that school ; and the period when he became a governor he (Major Pickmere) remembered very well. He thought it was one of the most touching sights he had ever seen in Warrington when his lordship's remains were carried to their last resting place, accompanied by the sympathy and bowed heads, of, he might say, nearly all Warring- ton. It was like the sun setting into silence and peace. 80 years ago, he remembered, the school was a very different place from what it was now: the education was very much different. The school, as he well remembered it, was a building very similar in outline to the pre- sent one. Major Picktnere described some of the features of the former building and humorously cited some reminiscences of an old arm chair with squeaking casters in the school, associated in his mind with the punishment of the boys because the head master used to push the chair aside when a boy was sent up to him, and referred to his own experience of the application of " strap oil." Warrington, he said, then was a very different place from what it was now. The schoolttoys of that day had not the means of enjoy, rig themselves that they had to-day. They had no cricket or football club; the recreation of Warrington school- boys in those days was fishing in the river, and certainly that was a very nice enjoyment, because at that time the river was pretty full of fish. Ha often went from that school to the island in the weir to see the salmon trying to jump over the weir: they would never see that now. (Laughter.) The scholars now had every advan- tage, learning not only Latin and Greek but all the modern languages, mathematics, and a host of other things, so that if the lads did not become very learned r they ought to do. The principal things that the boys learnt when he was one of them were Latin and Greek, varied occasionally by Greek and Latin. (Laughter). They had about a couple of hours a week for reading and arithmetic. He could see one or two persons there, that day who learnt Latta in the school at that time, who were not very famous for their handwriting, which was sometimes very difficult to read. He thanked Mr. Willcocks for giving them so able a report, and he was very glad to hear that the school was so successful, and that the Warrington boys had a pride in that school and did their utmost for its interests, which they certainly had done lately by gaining so many scholarships and fellowships. He was very much obliged to Mr. Willcecks for asking him to present the prizes on that occasion, and he hoped the school would be prosperous in the future as it had been in the past. (Applause.) Mr, WILLCOCKS said he was much obliged to Major Pickmere for his interesting speech about the old cus- toms of the school.

Subsequently Master S. Walton read part of his prize essay on "The making of England," and Master H. K. Gornall, ma., part of his prize Latin essay "Teutons ad Christum versi," which were well read and ranch applauded. Other bymns, and some English songs were sung by the boys in very creditable style, and a German and a French play were performed by a number of she scholars. The German play was entitled " Suchet so werdet ihr finden " the characters being as follows : —Roll (gentleman), E. S. Kidd ; Bertha (his niece) S. Walton ; Eugen Von Hoendorf, J. R. Evans; Frank Berner, C. H. Ferguson ; Duft (Roll's gardener), R. D. Willcocks. The name of the French play was "En Tigre du Bengale," (A Bengal Tiger,") the cast of which was as follows :—Pont-Aux-Choux (gentlemkn), J. H. Wright ; Aurelie (his wife), E. W. Coates ; Cerfeuil (their neighbour), H. K. Gornall ; Clapotte (their servant) J. S. Wallace.
The pieces were given very creditably, the female parts being carried out inest realistically by the boys who performed them.

div.head: SENTENCE OF DEATH.
div.p: SENTENCE OF DEATH.

John George Wensel, aged 25 years, a German butcher, was indicted at the Central Criminal Court, London, on Wednesday, for the murder of Detective Joyce. He was also charged with shooting Henry Selzer and Frederick Buhmann. Prisoner was suspected of a rob- bery at Dalston, and upon Joyce and the two other men endeavouring to arrest him he fatally shot Joyce and wounded the others. For the defence Mr. Geoghegan urged the jury to reduce the crime from murder to man- slaughter. No doubt Joyce was a gallant and good officer. There was a severe struggle prior to the shots being fire, and he submitted that the firing was accidental and that there was no intention of inflicting injury, !much less of committing murder. The jury found prisoner guilty, and he was sentenced to death.

The first part of the proceed- ings was a rnosical entertainment by the students which was excellently rendera. The DEAN of Manchester then distributed prizes and suhsequently addressed the students. He observed that although the report of the Examiner was not yet pub- lished, the Rector, their secretary, told him that the I school was in every respect very satisfactory. He said , the stodents would have great advantages in life as coming from the home of the clergy, they were being taught, no doubt, by the example of their parents and by the instructions they were given. They therefore started life under pleasant auspices when they came there, prepared in some sort for their ' training as they had come from homes where they would be under some discipline. He regretted that many on leaving school utterly gave up all their read- ing, and led a dissipated life as regarded their reading. He hoped that when they left school they would not throw away their reading. He deprecated the reading of nothing but novels, and said it behoved than not to lose interest in their stores of history. He trusted that they would maintain their character; let them be true to it, and if they were inspired by God they would be true. (Applause.) The following is the TRIER LIST. Form V. THE LUNCHEON. After the latter part of the programme had been cone through, the students and their friends partook of lun- cheon, provided by the authorities of the College, in the dining hall.—General Sir Richard Wilbraham proposed the health of the Dean of Manchester and all interested 'in that excellent institution. Ile impressed upon the , students the mistake it would be if far a moment they concluded that their education finished when they left the co:lege. In fact it was only just beginning. It was there that they "learned to learn." Be was on foreign service with his regiment before he was seventeen, and he was neither at a public school nor college. But he had always been fond of study, and he id not even feel at his age Ohat his education had by any means ceased. —The Dean of Manchester responded, and highly com- plimented Miss Beal, the headmistress, for her earnest ness, and devotion for the welfare of the students.—The Rector proposed the health of Miss Beal. lie remarked be did not think it possible for them to find a more con- scientious head-mistress and one more kindhearted and loving. She was always thinking about the good of the girls, and their real happiness.—The Rev. Chas. Winslow I responded on behalf of Miss Beal. He said he felt unable to express the thanks owing to her for her kindness and devotion to that institution.—The Rev. J. A. M. John- stone proposed the toast of "Success to the school," and the company then dispersed.

resignation to the proper authority for acceptance itt the hands of her Majesty. (Applause.) t 1,,• had been associated with that movement from the first, and it was a great wrench to him to tear himself away from the battalion and the number of friends he had invari- ably found in it. He had never had more kindness and consideration shown him from anyone or in any place than he:liad received from the voltinteers since he had been associated with them in Warrington, and he would tell them this, with perfect truth, that the happiest days of his life had been spent in that regiment. He should retire feeling the great severance which his resignation would occasion. at the same time he should retire into private life believing that be carried with him their i respect—he hoped he might be allowed to say it, because 1 e did feel it towards them—the respect and esteem of very man in that regiment. (Cheers.) But while he It pain and sorrow at parting from them, he hoped to ntinue in some way associated with that regiment. Cries of" Hear, hear.") It had been his first love,, and e intended it to be his last, and so long as there was a kick in him he hoped to be associated with them as the 1(141, true, good men he had always found them to be. (Charts.) A man ought to leel proud of commanding such noble, true-hearted men as he had always found those who, had done him the honour of serving with him as their commanding officer. (Loud cheers.) The volunteers then dispersed. CND RCH PARADE. I SU,' . `. the vol ' to the iber of

On Sunday morning, volunteers, numL._ about 150, marched from the Drill Hall to the Parish Church. Captains Ridgway, Buckton, Ede'sten, Baynes. and Hutchinson, Captain and Adjutant Adam, Lieutenants Chorley and Fairclough, Major Lister, and Surgeon- Major Adams. The Rector preached, from the Ist of Jeremiah, sth c. In the course of his sermon he asked if they would have been present that morning had they not been Volunteers? Would they as a matter of course have been found in the House of God, worshipping Him ? Lot them walk through the streets of Warrington any Sunday, and see whether men realized what God's day was. Let them as heads of families set an example. As grown-up men they were able to do what they chose, but an awful responsibility rested upon them, and it was their duty to set an example to the rising generation. Were things as they should be in that town ? Was there that spirit of soberness, temperance, and chastity which ought to exist amongst them ? Were there not those who were a disgrace to their humanity, a.though they were men made in the image and likeness of God? The existence of intemperance had been a reproach to their town for a long time ; let them, therefore, strive after a spirit of temperance. He trusted them as citizens; as well as from a national point of view. As they knew, the country was passing through a great crisis. A new Parliament was about to meet. They knew, too, that , more people had votes now than was formerly the case, I and in all probability that number would be increased in , the time to come. He wanted them all, therefore, to endeavour to realize their responsibility in the matter. There were two great parties in politics at the present time in the land. He wished to ascribe to each the highest motives; and when he spoke of these matters in the House of God it was only from the highest point of view. The rev, gentleman said he could speak of the Warring- ton Volunteers in terms of praise, for they knew that he was with them when they encamped by the seaside. It was the one week of tropical weather they had had this I summer, and he was struck with the endurance of the men. He looked at them under the blazing sun, but he heard no complaints ; they were quite quite patient, and endured the heat bravely and good-temperedly. Great endurance, he thought, there was, and they recollected the General's word of praise. They were not words of flattery, and he was sure they were thoroughly deserved on account of their endurance, their obedience, and their smartness.—After the service the volunteers were marched back to the Drill Hall, and then dispersed.

div.head: COLLIER DROWNED. FATAL RESULT OF A DRINKING BOUT.
div.p: A COLLIER DROWNED. FATAL RESULT OF A DRINKING BOUT.

On Saturday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Ship Inn, !Lades- town, relative to the death of Richard Jackson, thirty-six years of age, a collier residing at Arnold's Cottages, Haydock, who was found drowned on Friday morning last in the Sankey and St. Helens Canal at Earlestown. _

Peter Hughes, a collier, residing near deceased. stated that he met the deceased on Friday evening, the 15th inst., about seven o'clock. They went to a public-house kept by a man named Sharpies, and had two or three glasses of beer each. They left there about twenty minutes past eight, and walked to the Ship Inn at Earles- town, where they stayed until closing time. Witness said he had no idea how much beer they had to drink, and he could not recollect what door they left the house by. He admitted they must have been drunk. He remembered walking along the canal bank towards home. Before they got to the highway they both lay down and fell asleep. Witness awoke about one ofclock in the morning, and found that he was wet through, owing to the heavy fall of rain. De- ceased was lying near him. He tried to arouse him, but could not, and left him on the canal bank, and went home. He (witness) got home about two o'clock in the morning, and did not know the deceased had not come home until the following morning. Witness said that he remembered one of them purchasing a quart bottle of beer in the Ship Inn, but he could not recollect which of them paid for it. He found it in his pocket when he awoke on the canal bank. The last thing he remembered in the house was that he asked the deceased to go home about twenty minutes to ten o'clock, but he refused. Jane Hayes, the landlady of the Ship Inn, said that the men were only served with two glasses of beer each, and that when they left they were not drunk. They got up when requested to leave, and walked straight when leaving. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned," the foreman remarking that he thought the men had had too much drink in the house.

„ The Coroner said that was his opinion, hut they were there only to find the cause of death. Mr. Inspector Kelly, who represented the police, had hoard the evi- dence, and he could take further proceedings if he desired.
