div.p: ,TINJUNFEER INSPECT[ON. RETIIit?.MENF OF COLONEL GREE.NALL.

In consequence of the volunteer brigade encamp- ment at Conway last. Whitsuntide being held at a less convenient time for tha Warrington members of the battalion than was the time at which the regimentaF.eamps were. formerly held, namely, in Walking Day Week, there was not a muster of two- thirds of the regiment. Hence, according to the rules, to ensurri due efficiency, a subeequent inspeC, tioti Of the; Warrington volunteers became neces- sary,. and this was held on Saturday afternoon, in a field belonging to •Sir Gilbert Greenhill, adjoining the football field in Wilderepool-road. The volun- teers, tot the number of 408, including the G Com- pany frotillfewton,wertatilrat drawn up in marching array in the Park, on the piece of ground opposite the Town Hall, and than, accompanied by their bugle and brass bands, marched to the in- spection ground, where they were reviewed by Twentyman, C.B. The weather was delightfully fine, and the scene, presenting the contrast of the bright green grass with the red uniform, was an inspiriting and picturesque one. The following officers were present in addition to the inspecting Colonel t—Colonel Greenall, commanding officer, Captains Ridgway, 13uckton, Baines, Eddelsten, and Widdowes, Sergt.-Major Lister, Surgeon.-Captain Adams, Lieutenants Chorley and Fair- dough, Captain and Quartermaster Hutchinson, Capt. and Adjutant F. A. AdarnaMergt.-biajor Fenaelly, Sergt.- Instructors Birch and Sullivan, Quartermaster-Sergt. Mycock, Quartermaster-Sergt. Watmough, Bandmaster Armstrong, Sergt.-Bugler Plinston, Hospital Sergeant Buckley, Sergt. Master-Cook Cliffe, and Pioneer-Sergt. Warburton. The review commenced about half-past five, when Colonel Greenall formed the men from column into line, after which there was the general salute, and then the march past which was done in excellent order. Capt. Ridgeway afterwards put the men through manual and firing exercises,and Colonel Greenall then again took them in hand,Captains Widdowes, Buckton, Baines, and Edelsten successfully putting them through various inanceuvres. Colonel Twentyrnan then addressed the men. He said he was very much pleased with the bat- talion. They had drilled very steadily, much more so than on previous occasions. He was very glad they had been to the camp at Conway. When they had been in brigade camp two or three times he had no doubt they would get out of that groove that a regiment must always get into when drilled at a regimental camp , simply, for the mixing up with different regiments gave them better insight into matters and tended to promote efficiency. The march past might have been better if there had not been a ditch that was just opp)site the saluting flag. The placing of the flag there was the fault of the man who had selected the ground as if ha had first looked about a little he would very soon have seen a better place. After the address the men were again arrayed in marching order by Colonel Greenall and they proceeded to the drill hall, the bands playing the regi- mental air, which had also been struck up during the march past " God bless the Prince of Wales." On their arrival at the Hall they were addrested by the Com- manding ()Meer.

Colonel GREENALL said he wished to say a few words to them before dismissing them. First of all,he wanted to speak about the drill that day. The inspection had passed off very well, and the movemnits had all been very steadily made. The men had turned out very well, very clean, their uniform looking well and the accoutre- ments properly adjusted. He might say without flattery as to the first movement that of standing at attention, with shouldered arms, and with the Colonel riding down the ranks, that he never saw any regiment look better, or stand More steadily. (Applause.) It was also noticed by Colonel Twentywian as he rode down the ranks. He (Colonel Greenall) was very sorry that the musters had not been during the past week what they might have been, Many men in the ranks that day had evidently not at- tended many drills, and Many WPM in the ranks wha were not in camp. It was a pity they could not all manage to come up when they went into camp, because they were able to distinguish between those who had not been in camp and those who had not; the line of the re- giment showed that at once. Those who were not in camp might have arranged to have come up for instruc- tion during the past week. The muster that day was very much smaller than many musters of the regiment at which he had been present, but that was accounted for chiefly, he supposed, by the fact that the regiment was numerically weak. They were at the present moment, he was sorry to say, much weaker, he be- lieved, than they had ever been, but he was happy to tell them at the same time, that he believed the stuff of the regiment was never better than at the present time. (Applause.) They would not have the pleasure of seeing Colonel Twentyman any more as their inspecting officer, as his time would very soon be up, and he was about to retire into private life, to rest which he had well earned. They had always found him very kind and nice. When he had found fault he had always done it in a kind and sollierly manner, and they would all regret, he was sure, his resignation. Then there was another rather disagreeable matter to mention. This was the last in- spection that the Adjutant would be present at. He was sorry to say that his time would be up in January, so that they would have the benefit of his presence at the annual inspection again, but he personally felt very sorry that they would be deprived of his services thereafter, and he could not thank him enough for his attention to his duties, and the admirable way in which he had per- formed everything entrusted to his charge. (Applause.) He agreed with that; the Adjutant deserved that applause ' and more of it if it came to that. Then he had to mention another disagreeable thing, that they would not have , again on parade Sergeant-Instructor Birch. His time was up with the battalion, and he was going to take up some business, which he was sure they all hoped would be very successful and prosperous. At the same time they were very sorry to lose his services. (Applause.) He had always found him most zealous and conscienti- ous in the discharge ef his duty, and he should regret his loss very much. (Applatse.) Arlether matter which he wished to mention was the great loss the bat- talion had sustained in the death of Lord Winmarleigh, a nobleman who had been connected with that corps from the day of its birth. He had taken the greatest possible interest in the battalion. Colonel Wilson-Patten,. as he then was, Was one of the first subscribers to the fund required to form the corps. The Volunteer movement was not so popular in those days as now, and they had very few friends to go to, but Colonel Wilson-Patten came forward and nobly subscribed £lOO to start the corps. And not only that, but whenever they had bazaars ts raise funds for the benefit of the corps he was one of the first and foremost to come forward, invari- ably attending those ha/. tars and spending money freely. He felt that they could not readily replace Lord Win- marliegh in the battalion, as not only was he a good friend to all of them, but he was proud to say he was a personal friend of his, and he had never had a warmer hearted, more attached, and sincere friend than he found in Lord Winmarleigh. Be wished to announce, and he did so with the deepest possible regret, accom- panied with pain, that it was his intention to forward, on the 25th of September. after having completed 33 years as commanding officer (it that regiment, his

div.head: NEW GLAZEBROOK RIFLE itAliCiE,
div.p: THE NEW GLAZEBROOK RIFLE itAliCiE,

The Warrington Volunteers—the Ist V.B. (P.W.V.) South Lancashire Regiment—are, like many another volunteer battalion, handicapped by want of a sufficiently large and a sufficiently accessible shooting range. At present they :Moot over a range in the vicinity of Widnes, but in time they are to be admitted to the advantages of the proposed Manchester ranges at Glazebrook as soon as the land on Rixton Moss,that has already been secured, has been properly reclaimed and solidified. The scheme, of course, is entirely a Manchester one, but Warrington has been admitted to a share, and in this connection it is stated that the late Lord Win- znarleigh, a firm supporter of the volunteer move- ment, of whose estate the Moss formed a portion, stipulated that the men from Warrington should participate in the advantages. Captain Ridgway and ' other officers of the Warrington corps have taken great interest in the scheme since its incep`ien, and the former has from time to time kept the battalion in- formed as to its progress. The strip of land to be used is 213 acres in extent, and is between Glazebrook and Warrington, say about a mile and a half from Glazebrook station. It will be very easily accessible either from Manchester or Warrington, and the Cheshire Lines Committee are going to do things handsomely by pro- viding a siding and station accommodation close to the place, and by running convenient trains at reduced fares. It is estimated that it will take twelve ' months to thoroughly drain and reclaim the bog, which is over twelve feet in depth, and will not be solidified until great expense has been incurred. Indeed some £2,000 have already been paid by the battalions joined in the scheme, and it is stated that £15,000 in all will be required to equip the range, that sum having to be borrowed under the Range Act of 1891, on the security of the capital grant, to be repaid with interest at the rate of 3i Der cent. The payment will be spread over 2.5 years, and he battalions, according to their strength, will take the responsibility. The Manchester brigade is the first to avail itself of the borrowing powers men- tioned, and the committee, composed of 18 officers,have had a good deal of care and anxiety in regard to the matter. A great deal of work will have to be done in the way of raising mounds, placing target machinery, and building huts for the markets The mere mention of the fact that accommodation for fl,OOO men will be provided is enough to indicate the magnitude of the scheme. The battalions concerned are :-3rd V.B. The Lancashire Fusiliers (afford), eight companies; Ist V.B. The Manchester Regiment (half at Wigan), twelve com- panies ;2nd ditto, thirteen companies :4th ditto thirteen companies; sth ditto twelve companies; Ist V. 8., the Prince of Wales's Vohinteers (Warrington)six companies. Longitudinally the full distance over which firing rights have been secured is a little over two miles.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY AFFRAY.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY AFFRAY.
ALLtgED FO-ACHING. A FIGHT WITH BLUDGEONS.

On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, before Mr. Chas. Reynolds and Mr. Alfred Thomas, three young men named John Davies, jun., Arnold William Davies, and Frederick Davies, sons of Mr. John Davies, farmer, Bird's Wood Farm, Aston by Sutton, were summoned by Samuel Tomlinson, 'heal-keeper to Mr. H. Talbot, J.P.. of Dutton Lodge, for night poaching at Aston by Sutton, on the 19th July.—Mr., A. Linaker appeared to prosecute, and Mr. H. Jenkins, of NI arrington, defended. Mr. Linaker Said Mr. Jenkins ban told him that he would prove. that the defendants had authority from the occupier of the land to be there; that being so his instruc- tions were to withdraw the summone.—nr. Jenkins asked the Bench not to allow Mr. Linaker to with- draw the summons, but to dismiss it. Here were three respectable young men, sons of a respectable tenant of the estate charged through their own landlord with night poaching: it was not fair to prefer such a serious charge against the sons of a man who had been a good and honourable tenant, and then come to that Court and ask to be allowed to withdraw. His clients were , justified by law in what they did. The Game Laws I Amendment Act laid down that the prima facie right to kill game was in the tenant, and the only pnesible way of taking that right away from the tenant was by a proper contract made between landlerd and tenant by which that right was reserved without qualification to the landlord. Mr. Davies had been occupier of the farm for over 27 years. Twenty-seven years ago he took a four- teen years' lease and in that lease there was a proper reservation of game. From the time of the expiration of the lease other contracts were made by which a new tenancy was created. The old landlords died and the estate became invested in the Court of Chancery, and there had since been no new contract vesting the reser- vation of game in Mr. Talbot; but there had been nothing done to prevent Mr. Talbot having a reasonable enjoyment in killing ;aerie over the farm.—Mr. Linaker said he withdrew the summonses because until now they were not aware that the teriaet had authorised the three defendants to be on the land to take rabbits. If they had known before they would not have issued any sum- mons for poaching.—Mr. Jenkins said the Bench would recognise the ridiculousness of this position. Here was a father with three sons was be to go to the landlord and ' say " If vou please; my three sons are going to catch rabbits ?" (Laughter.)—Mr. Linaker said they had not been informed .41 any authority whatever.—After a con- sultation the Bench dismissed the case, and Mr. Jenkins then applied for costs.—The Bench allowed half-a-crown to each defendant and to the father and the advicates fee of 10s. 6d., total £IO. &I.—Jas. Tomlinson sen., Jas. Tomlinson jun., (gamekeeper), and James Woodier, were then charged with assaulting Arnold W. Davies; Joseph Lewis, Joseph Wilkinson, and James Tomlinson jun., were summoned for assaulting Frederick Davies; and James Tomlinson see., and W. Chas. Wilkinson were summoned for assaulting John Davies jun. ; John Davies, Arnold W. Davies, and Frederick Davies were summoned for assaulting James Tomlinson.—Mr. Jenkins, in opening the case for the brothers Davies, said on the night of the 19th inst., the young men, in pursuance with their father's authority, went into a field which adjoins Bird's Wood. This wood was very much infested with rabbits, and Mr. Davies having for a considerable time sustained serious lose through crops being devoured by rabbits, and Seeing unable to obtain any compensation, ho exercised the authority vested in him, and he directed his sons to take such measures as they thought necessary to destroy these rabbits. On the night in question they went to this field, and Aibll and Arnold fired a net and Fred went to heat up the rabbits. They caught three rabbits. After they had been there eOlert tillle 11V4 bend the eQUnd of men coming, kill he Went and told ilia brothers that the keepers were coming. They stood there, and they heard Joseph Wilkinson say to the head keeper, Tomlinson, " Draw it James" (meaning the net). John Davies then said " let any man touch it, or dare." The keeper—whom it was plain to be seen had been assaulted and he (Mr. Jenkins) said serve him right—the keeper said " Oh you are on for that sort of work are you ?" and he at once struck at John Davies with a big thick stick, but he did not sue- eeed. John then struck at Tomlinson, but did not hit birn, and the latter rushed at John, took him by the throat, and maltreated him. What occurred afterwards could better be described as a melee. Arnold Davies who was commonly known as Roger was struck down and rendered unconscious and the defendants tied his bands, and dragged him badly injured and bleeding as, he was, to Dutton Lodge. In getting over a fence they dropped him into the bottom of a ditch. When they arrived at the Lodge they said "Oh Roger is that you," and there was some expression of regret, and some one really had the courtesy to untie his hands, and another fetched him a drop of brandy. Mr. Talbot made use of expressions.—Mr. Linaker objected to anything about Mr. Talbot being introduced, he was not summoned.—Mr. Jenkins said he would not say anything with regard to Mr. Talbot ; something could be said but he would . refrain. Mr. Jenkins character- ised the assault as a most brutal, and asked that the 'defendants should receive the punishment they deserved I with a view to the protection of public rights.—John Davies gave evidence of a corroborative character. Arnold Wm. Davies said he was struck on the head and 'knocked senseless. He did not know who did it. He lost a great deal of blond. His hands were tied and the two Tomlinsons took him towards Dutton Lodge. The other four men walked behind. In getting over a fence Tomlinson senior pulled him into the ditch. At Dutton Lodge Tomlinson said " You are a nice neighbour to strike me in that fashion." He (witness) replied " I did not strike you " and Tomlinson said "1 don't think you have, it must have been Kelly that I had." Kelly was employed by his father. Mr. Talbot called witness " A d-- poacher" and flourished his fist in his face several times. He gave him in custody of the policeman and said he would give his (witness's) father notice to quit the farm. He had been under the doctors hands up to the present time.—Fred Davies said he was struck at but was not hit. He ran away and was followed by three men who set a collie dog upon him.— John Davies, the father, said on the 21st he met Wood- ward who said " I am very sorry about this affair that occurred the other night. We all Know we have been in the wrong but they fetched me out of bed and compelled me to go." He replied "Perhaps you will be sorrier before it is finislied."—Mr. Linaker said he appeared for Tomlinsim and the other men. Tomlinson had instruc- tions to keep down rabbits in Bird's Wood, and on the night in question Tomlinson and the other men turned out to carry out this object. When crossing the Old Park Field in the occupation of Mr. Davies,they saw three forms draw up together but could not recognise them as it was very dark. Tomlinson went to within a few yards from them and called out three times " Who are you," and received no reply. Tomlinson then called up"' Now, lads come up, we must know who they are," or words to that effect. One of them called out " Stand Iblacfc," and then the three jtunped over the net and set OR Tomlinson who was about a yard in advance of the other five. Tomlinson warded off the blows as well as he could, and hi the scrimmage dropped his stick, but he caught hold of the man nearest to him and dragged him some yards away. While doings() the man struck him on the face and when struggling together someone came behind him and dealt him a fearful blow on the back of the head, which brought him down. He was dazed and lost his grasp of the prisoner who got away. Both these men ran up the field. On getting beck to the other men. Tomlinson found they had captured a man,and he bound his wrists with loose rope handcuffs and started with him to Dutton Lodges. The prisoner kept Saying " James where are you taking me," but net in a voice they could tell who he was, and he did not disclose his I name or the names of those who were with him. When they got into the light at Dutton Lodge, Tomlinson knew the man and said" I am surprised at you Roger ; why didn't you speak when I asked you and it would have saved all this bother. The witnesses would deny that a blow was struck before they were attacked, and then what took place was simply a scuffle between the men Woodward, Lewis and Tomlinson and the three men who I attacked them. The other men stood behind under the circumstances that the men did not reply when challenged. He asked that a severe example should be made of them.—James Tomlinson senior corroborated the advocates statement. He did not recognize the men at all ; and they struck the first blows. He denied that he pulled Arnold Davie., into a ditch. They struck two matches with the object of seeing who Arnold Davies was, hut through the high wind they could not get them alight.—The other men gave evidence showing that they were first attacked, and that they did not know their assailants.—Ths magistrates retired to consider their decision, and on returning into Court Mr. Reynolds said his colleague and he could not agree upon this case so they arrived at no decision.—Mr. Jenkins suggested that the sum- monses should be adjourned and reconsidered before another Bench. Mr. Linaker said he should leave himself perfectly free to take his own course in future.—Mr. Ashton the Magistrates' Clerk) said if the case was to be reheard fresh summonses must be issued.

RUNCORN BARMAN AT LIVERPOOL RACES. EXCITING RAILWAY ADVENTURE.

On Monda". at the Lity'PoliT Court, Liyekpool, before Mr. 11. J. Cook, two respectably-dressed men, named John Ward and Bernard Magee, the latter of whom is a well-known Liverpool boxer, were placed in the doek charged on remand with assaulting and Irobbing William Henry Smith, on the 21st inst.„: whilst in a railway carriage travelling between 1 Aintree and Liverpool on the Lancashire and -; Yorkshire Railway. Mr. Cunliffe (Bellringer and. Cunliffe) prosecuted on behalf of the Lancashire z' and YorkAhire Railway Company, and prisoners ; were undefended. The prosecutor, who is a barman,l residing with his father at the Duke of Wellington ° Hotel, Percival-lane, Runcorn, stated that at about 5.50 p.m. on the 215 t inst. he, in company with two friends, entered a third-class compartment at Aintree Station, after coming from the races. Shortly afterwards the prisoners entered the rompartment, Ward setting him- self beside him, and Magee opposite him. They then appeared to be sober, and he (witness) was also sober. Shortly after the train started, Magee used some filthy language towards prosecutor. He told them that he did not want anything ta do with them, whereupon Magee got hold of him by the shoulders and butted him in the mouth with his head. Prosecutor then got up from his seat, when Ward grasped his hands from behind, at the same time putting his hand into his (witness's) left- hand watch pocket, which had previou dy contained £5 in gold. Magee then butted him again in the face. 'Witness cried out that be had been robbed. and Magee said, "pitch him out of the window." Upon arrival at Sandhills, which was the first stopping Plaele. Ward got out of the carriage, and prosecutor followed him into the street, and gave him in ohar4e of Police- constable 262 E (Hunt). Witness had not yet recovered the money.—ln answer to the charge, Ward said, " I did not steal the money, hut I will do for him yet."—The prisoner Magre was arrested the following evening in Lime-street by Detective Sub-Inspector R•bbins, and when charged at the Detective Office said he knew I • nothing about it. He was drunk at the time and did not be!ieve that he was in a railway train—After hear- ing corroborative evidence, prisoners were committed to the assizes for trial.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY TRAGEDY IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY TRAGEDY IN SCOTLAND.
TWO PERSONS KILLED.

A Glasgow correspondent telegraphs that James Fraser, a bank clerk, rushed into a house at nine o'clock on Tuesday night at Belmont, midway between Olaagow and Edinburgh, and with a sword killed William Shadwell, waiter at Blair Lodge Academy, and then assaulted Shadwell'e wife in such a way that her removal to the Edinburgh Infirmary was necessary. Fraser afterwards attacked a young woman on the highway and killed her. He has been apprehended. It appears that abut nine o'clock William Shadwell and his wife4essie Tait or Shadwell, were sitting in their house, when they were alarmed by the entrance of a neighbour named James Fraser, a bank clerk, residing at Valview, who rushed into the house with a sword in his hand. It is stated that Fraser first struck Mr. Shad well and then turned upon and attacked Mrs. Shad- well. Ilii.band and wife ran out of the house, and were followed by Fraser into the garden, where it is alleged, the latter attacked Mrs. Shadwell a second time, felling her to the ground. Thereupon her husband rushed between thtni lC; prevent further violence. [Was again struck by Fraser 3tll linnirea aowh, Mrs. Shadwell, airtime: severely weainded, was able to make her way to a neighbouring house, but her husband was fatally wounded and died shortly after- wards. Fraser then, it is alleged, went out into the roadway, where he attacked a young woman named Mary Grindley, who was passing at the time. It is re- ported that he struck her on the head repeatedly with a sword. The unfortunate young woman was imme- mediately removed to her mother's house, but suc- cumbed to her injuries within three or four minutes Mrs. Fraser meantime went to the spot and managed to induce her husband to go indoo-s, where the police sub- sequently discovered him sitting in a chair, hold- ing a sword in one hand and a revolver in the other. fie did not appear at all inclined to be violent or to resist his arrest. It was found that he had been severely, wounded in the thigh, and after the injury had been attended to he was removed to Falkirk, where he was !ticked up. Fraser was well supplied with ammuni- tion, his pockets being filled with cartridges, and he also was in possession of two revolvers. Dr. Wickham wag summoned to the scene of the outrage, and under his instructions Mrs. Shadwell was removed to Falkirk Cottage Hospital, suffering from serious injuries to the head, arm, and thigh, and there seems some danger that these wounds, added to the shock to the system, may result fatally. At present the poor woman is unaware of the fate of her husband. Fraser and Shadwell are said to have been on the very best terms, and it is ! alleged that when the former attacked the husband and wife Mr. Shadwell exclaimed, " Oh Mr. FlaSer, what do ! you mean by this ?" His assailant vouchsafed no reply.

div.head: POISONING IN IRELAND.
div.p: POISONING IN IRELAND.

The Irish police have arrested a woman named Macalis- ter, and her daughter, a girl of ten years, on suspicion of being concerned in a poisoning afflir which occurred on Saturday evening, at Cushendall, county Antrim. Fiveyoung children were taken suddenly ill, and one died after a few hours. The arrests were made in con- sequence of statements by the survivors.

div.head: TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
div.p: TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

Melton Mowbrav was on Monday afternoon the scene of a railway disaster attended by lOFS of life. A passen- ger train ran of! the line a few 'itindred yards from the Great Northern Station and the North-Western Junction, and was precipitated down an embankment, the car- riages rolling into a brick-yard. The driver and stoker of the train and a Melton Mowbray newsboy were killed.
SHOCKING TRAGEDY IN IRELAND.

On Sunday morning, at a hamlet a few miles from liallyfarnnn, County Roacommon, a woman who had been of unsound mind for some time past put her three children heads downwards into a large pot of boiling water, and 'called them to death. She afterwards at- tempted suicide hr putting her head into the same pot, and was so shockingly scalded that there areno hopes of her recovery.

div.head: EXECUTION AT DEVIZE;4.
div.p: EXECUTION AT DEVIZE;4.

John Gurd was executed at Devizes on Tuesday morning for the murder of Itenry Richards at Melksham on April 9, and of Police-sergeant Moulden on April 12. Richards was murdered because Gurd believed he was instrumental in inducing his niece, Florence Adams, to break off her engagement to marry Gurd, and the police- sergeant was shot while (lord was endeavouring to escape arrest by the sergeant, a superintendent, and two gonstables, Gurd firing two shots at the police with the revolver with which he had shot Richards.

The mining division of the Labour Commission met on Tuesday in London, under the presidency of Mr. Dale and heard evidence regarding the conditions of work at Dinorwic Quarries, the Hon. W. W. Vivian,. manager director, presenting the case of the owners. Mr. W. Abraham, M.P.,tho Welsh miners' representa- tive, on Tuesday resigned his position as miners' agent, in order, it is explained, to test the miners on the sliding scale question, there being a reat division of opinion among the men regarding the advisability of continuing the agreement. Mr. Abraham is strongly in favour of tile sliding scale arrangement, with souse amendtnent on its terms. It was announced on Tuesday that Messrs. Edward Mortal! and Sons, worsted spinners, Morton Mill, Bing- ley, bad called a meeting of their creditors. The liabi- lities are said to amount to £120,000, and the assas to about £BO,OOO.

At Greenwich Police Court, on Tuesday, Alfred Crock- well and his wife were charged, under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, with procuring a girl named Alice Shead, aged sixteen, and were remanded, bail being al- lowed.

During some naval manceuvres off Brest, on Monday night, a t ornedo boat steamed right on te the ram of an Wended, and sank in ten fathoms of water. The crew were saved. An entire family, nine persons in all, were drowned at Wheeling,West Virginia,on Monday night, by a cloud- burst, which also destroyed roads and washed away bridges and railroads. About 300 buildings, four hotels, two churches, and fifty shops have been destroyed by fire at Bay City, Michigan, the value of property destroyed being esti- mated at 1,000,000 dols. So far as could be learned, only one life was lost. The eruption of Mount Etna was more violent on Tuesday than during the past few days. On Monday night a shock of earthquake wee experienced at thirty- seven miles to the south of the volcano. - - -

. • THE Ministry are beginning to see Looking Ahead that it looks rather ridiculous of . , of them not to resign when they have been beaten at the polls. They will, IdOw- eVer, meet Parliament; they. will be out-votsrl,and they will be turned out. This is in . the oi•dinary. course of things; but they hope against hope that Orriething will happen to interfeva With the ordi- nary course: of things.' 'Lord 'BEACONSFIELD in One of his epigrammatic moods said "it is the unex-: 'pected which happens;" and the Tory Micawhers are waiting .for.something--they knew not what— to happen in their favour. They are of course "profoundly convinced" that MT:GLADSTONE will not be able to carry on the business of the country with a majority of 42; and yet they are in mortal dread of his falsifying their pre- dictions as he has so often done. According to their .theory, he was `!played out" a dozen years'ago ; then they 'had. it, in 1886, that he :would never again be, equal to the cares of office; but .here he is, in 1892, the 'one man who domi- Vat 4 tho situafion—the'one'' man who towers above all the rest. Last week the Tories were in a hurry to show. that a Majority, which was ob- tainesd by counting Irish members, Was not a -national majority ; bat 'they hate dropped this argument since it is borne in. Upon them that it savours of separation. Perhaps, too, they remem- ber that they had no objection to Trish votes when Mr. PARNELL issued his manifesto in 4400 ; and it may occur to them that the few Parnellites that are stillleft fritiY'even yet.btAiseful to( them in the House of Commons.. So, they are breaking fresh ground; it is being pointed out that Home Rule would. be a great constitutional change ; and that, if we look to America, we find that no amendment of the 'constitution can be made which is not approved by two-thirds of both Houses of Congress. But: American law is not English law; and, further, there is no com- parison' between the two cases. Most of the States in' America are large enough to be regarded as cOnntries in thems elves'; they -posse,* as such, large, independent authority—larger authority than Ireland ;seeks to obtain under Home Rule; 'and it is to preserve this independence that the two:-thirds majority is required. To Complete the analogy, Ireland should first be granted Home Rule powers, with a proviso that these powers shall not be interfered with except on the decision of a two-thirds majority of both Houses of Parlia- ment. How will that suit these - Tory logicians? There is this much certain about much that is uncertain as to the various rumours and pro- posals that are in the air, and that is that Mr. Gladstone will pay no attention to

tho advice which his eppoiient's may giVes Need we say that it would perhaps, be as well if own supporters were a trifle less fr!c with th‘it suggestions until the Liberal ;chief is actually in office? He does not speak out ju at now because, av "the old Parliatrientary hand," he knows that it wolild be imprudent, not to say indeci;ut, to mite' Parliamentary procedure until he is placectat, the head Of Parliament. When the Tories go out of office, they always leave a lock of their hair. This time, they are leaving two locks—in the shape of the Morocco difficulty and the Uganda trouble. -- It is amusing to observe our local Tory contem- Porary indulging in boasts about its "increased circulation," when it is known that free copies have been very freely distributed during the recent election campaign. A little less brag, and some- thing in the shape of dividend would be more eatisfactory to the shareholders.

*** In the " Examiner " for August 6th there will " be commenced a new Serial, entitled" lonie, the Pride of the Mill, by Laura Jean Libbey. This is a thrilling love story, pourtraying the life, romance, and strange fate of a lovely New York working-girl : and we can strongly re- commend it to our readers.

JOSEPH PRITCHARD. Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High. ,t., and 4, Bridge-st., ST. PAUL'S CHURCH CHOIR, WIDNES. The members of this choir had their annual picnic on Saturday, when they spent a pleasant time in Southport. The corntregation defrayed the expenses. Josi- MI PRITCHARD Is prepared to wind and keep In repair private clocks from 10s. per annum.--,lde. EXPLOSIVE STORES AT RUNCORN.

The Runcorn magistrates, on Monday, granted Mr. Wna. Edgar Lea a renewal of his license to store explo- sives at Weston and Bates Bridge, in buildings there constructed. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY. During the past month 12,473 persons have visited the reading-room and 4,209 books have been issued, being a considerable increase upon the figures of the correspond- ing month last year.

- DEATH OF Mns. WILLIAMS. OF llowouN. Mrs. Elizabeth Williams, of Percival Lane, widow of the late Mr. J. W. Williams, died on. Saturday morning after a protracted illness. She was highly respected. She was 39 years of age. If you wantyour watch repaired by skilful workmen. take It to PRITCH ARD'S.—Adrt. PAWNBROKERS' LICENSES AT R UNCO RN.

Go to PRITCHARD'S for the best five guinea watch a work- ingman can have.—Ado. BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The annual treat took place en We4nesday. Over 600 scholars, and teachers, &c., journeyed by special train to Frodsham at noon. and they marched in pro- cessional order to Mersey View, where a merry time was spent. Mr. John Simpson provided the numerous party with an excellent tea, and nuts, sweets, &c. were also distributed to the young people. , SUCCESSFUL WIDNES STUDENTS. The following were successful in passing the examina- tion in musical knowledge, held last month at St. George's Hall, Liverpool, in connection with Trinity College, London :—Miss Jessie Elizabeth Thomas, Deacon-road, 86 marks; Miss Maggie Thartne, Mill House, Ditton, 78 marks ; Miss Nellie Lewis, Cholmon- deley-street, 81 marks ; and Master William A. Buckley, Dickson-street, 61 marks. All the above were taught by Mrs. Martin, Widies. When in want of a chaste and elegant wedding or birthday present go to PRITCHARD'S, 51. High-st.—Advt. RUNCORN WATERMEN AND TIIEIR DEAD COMRADES. The members of the local branch of the Watermen's and Porters' Association have purchased,by subscription amongst themselves, a double grave in Runcorn Ceme- tery wherein to inter the remains of any one engaged in the canal trade who may die without means and without friends, so that they may have decent burial and not have a pauper's grave as their last resting place. The certificate of the grave is lodged with the secretary of the Watertnen's Association, Mr. Gatley, and the action of the members is to be commended.
JOSEPH PRITCHARD keeps spectacles to sui all sights Irons a shilling a pair.—Advt. _ A VIOLENT VAGRANT AT Itrwcortw. . _

At the Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Messrs. J. Brundrit and J. Handiey, John Davies, a stranger, was charged with sleeping in an outbuilding at Rtincorn, on Monday night, and further with assaulting P.C. Gregory. The officer on the date named, when in Canal-st. visited an outbuilding belonging to Mr. Horse- field, and found the prisoner there. The prisoner was drunk, and at once commenced to assault the officer by butting him. The officer was also kicked several times. Davies was committed to Knutsford Goal for seven days for the vagrancy, and for 14 dsys for the assault.

Hereby, clerk to the County Asylum, Chester, wrote informitg the "Board that there, Were only seven available beds On the'female side of thie house. botwithstanding the fact' that they had die- I charged some female patienta recently. Under 'the eir- cumsZances it would be well that relieving officers should enquire whether there was room before sending. any patient.—lt was decided that the Clerk should write to the Asylum authoritiei asking if there were not patient& in the asylum who had not an equal right to he there; as those from Runcorn Union as it was really al county institution. The Master reported that the child- ren had had their fourth annual excursion, and he had a balance left of £3 its. 6d. BRUTAL CONDUCT TO A WIFE AT WIDNES. Befcre Mr. B. Gaskell, jun., and Mr. T. H. Gossage, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Peter Kelly a powder packer, of Gladstone-street, was charged under a warrant *eh assaulting his wife Bridget Kelly, on Saturday last. The prisoner pleaded guilty. Mrs. Kelly said she was married to the prisoner near Manches- ter about 14 years ago, and three months later they removed to Widnes. During most of her married life the prisoner's conduct to her had been mast brutal. On Saturday last he came home the worse for drink, and without any provocation he beat her about the head and face with his fists.. In order to escape from his ferocious attack she ran out of the' house. The prisoner had sworn to take her life, and she lived in a state ot constant fear, and she asked that a separation order should be granted, There were six children of the marrir:le, the eldest being tmetee and the youngest two years. The prisoner was yen fond of the children. He was earning over £3 a week, ai.d !le asked for I.oi. a week and the custody of the ycungest child.—P.C. Almond and a neighbour gave evidence of the prisoner's brutality, the latter stat- ing the man was mad.—The prisoner said he acted under provocation as his wife WAS unfaithful to him, but Mrs. Kelly denied the charge.—The Bench sentenced the prisoner to 14 days' hard labour,and granted a judi- cial separation, the prisoner to contribute 10s. a week to his wife's support. Mrs. Kelly was given the custody of the youngest child. . PRITCIIAnD'S lotve now stood the test kr 50 years,and oual:ty and first-class workmanship are still guaranteed.—didet.
LAUNCH OF A FLAT AT RUNCORN.

A flat built by Mr. W. Bate at the Vine Yard was launched in the Bridgewater Canal on Thursday after- noon. The dimensions of the craft are 68 feet long, 14 feet three inches beam, and depth of hold five feet 10 inches. The carrying capacity is 60 tons with a draught of three feet eight inches. George Dawson is the name given to the fiat, which has boen built to the order of Messrs. Bate and Co., carriers between Liverpool and Manchester. RUNCORN POLICE NEWS. On Thursday morning, at Runcorn Police Court, before Messrs. J Brundrit and J. Handley, Charles Woods was charged under a warrant, he 'not having appeared to his summons on Monday, with being drunk on licensed premises at Halton, on the 2nd inst.—Fined 2s. 6d. and 13s. 4d. costs.—Sarah E. Jones, Wilson's- row, Runcorn, was ordered to pay Is. and 14s. costs, under a warrant for non-appearance to a summons on the 28th September last, for being drunk on the 12th of the month named.—Patrick Farrell and James Riley , were also fined for drunkenness.
BETHESDA. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, RUNCORN..

The re-opening services were continued on Sunday, when the Rev. Samuel Yates, of Spalding, formerly pastor of the church, delivered two eloquent sermons to large congregations. At the conclusion of the evening service Mr. A. G. Calvert, organist of Dring,houses Church, York, gave an organ recital. The performance included :—Offertoire in F (No. 5) (Wely) ; Andante in G (Batiste) ; grand chorus in D (Guilmant) ; Cujus Animam (Rossini) ; and Toccato in G (Dubois). Mr. Calvert tested the capabilities and qualities of the instru- ment to the full, and the concord of sweet sounds he ex- tracted by his skilful manipulation was highly enjoyed by the numerous audiences. Collections were taken in aid of the restoration fund. ACTION FOR THE Birx OF A DOG. At Widnes County Court, yesterday, before his Hon- our Judge Shand, Edward O'Neil, labourer, Water-st., sued Wm. Higy,inson, farmer, Carleton Terrace, Wines, for £9 damages alleged to have been sustained through the bite of a dog owned by the defendatit.—Mr. C. H. Lewin appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. J. W. Knowles defended. On the 3rd June the complainant and some friends were crossing a field near St. Mary's football ground, when the defendant came uo with a dog, and deliberately incited the animal to attack the plaintiff. He was bitten on the left leg and was not able to ftelow his employment for a fortnight, during which time he was under the care of Dr. Hutchinson.—The defendant said the plaintiff and three others were trespassing across a field of corn. He told them to go, off but they refused, contending that there formerly was a path across the field. He denied that he set the dog upon them or that the complainant was bitten.—His Honour said he was satisfied the dog was set on,and awarded the plaintiff £4 damages. SUCCESS OF RUNCORN MUSICAL STUDENTS.

Runcornians will be glad to hear of the success attained at Liverpool College by two sons of Mr. C. A. Timmins, of Ruckfield, Runcorn. Master Arthur Timmins has gained the Crown scholarship in connec- tion with the college, and his brother, Charles Timmins, held the second place in the same examination. Both the boys are in a junior form and the boaour is all the more meritorious as the scholarship has previously been invariably carried off by one of the senior boys. This success must be 'highly gratifying to the father, and reflects great credit upon their music teacher, Mr, Walter Burnett whom the Runcorn people will have an opportunity of hearing on the occasion f the c!ioir ser- mons at Trinity Church.—We are also pleased to record that the Trinity College (London), local examination in musical knowledge, has been successfully passed by Miss A. Smith, Grsenway Road (83 marks) and Master Arthur M. Poole, 135 Greenway Road(B9 marks). These results not only certify to the ability of the pupils but to the souud arid efficient training they have received from their tutor. Mr. William Cooke, of Church Place.
FREEMASONS' PICNIC FROM RUNCORN.

The annual picnic of the members of the Ellesmere Lodge of Freemasons took place on Thursday, when 43 ladies and gentlemen travelled from Widnes to Worksop by the Sheffield and Midland Railway. The party tra- velled by special train both going and returning, and two coaches were reserved for the party. Worksop was reached at 11.30, after a journey of three hours, and lunch having been partaken of at the Royal Hotel, the excursionists had a drive through charming country to Welheck Abbey, commonly known as " The Dukeries." the seat of the Duke of Portland. The afternoon was spent in a stroll through the extensive grounds ; an in- spection of the picture gallery, which contains some of the finest paintaings by both ancient and modern mas- ters ; a visit to the riding school, and a walk through the wonderful underground passages. Returning to Worksop, tea was partaken of, and starting for home at 7.20, Widnes was reached at ten o'clock. On the out- ward and return journey cabs were requisitioned be- tween Runcorn Bridge and the Central Station. Bro. Phillips, WM., accompanied the excursion.

, . , RUNCORN PARISI' CHURCH CHOIR. The annual sermons in aid of the choir funds of Run- corn Parish Church were preached on Sunday to good congregations. The Ven. Archdeacon of Chester was the morning preacher, and the pulpit was occupied in the evening by toe Rev. O. Hylton Stewart, M.A., vicar of New Brighton. The choir gave the anthems " Blessed I be thou, Lord God of Israel," and "Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way,'' in capital style. The solo poition was ably rendered by Mr. James Littler. the ' choirmaster. Mr. Jihnsois was at the organ. Subse- . (meat to the evening service, the Rev. C. Hylton Stewart, M.A.. gave an organ re;ital, and his admirable perform- ance was a source of great pleasure to the crowded con- ' g.regatioe. The collectioni realised £l4 14-t. 31, a Idecrease of £4 compared with last year. The juni or I members of the choir had their annual trip on Monday, when they travelled to Llandudno, under the ewe of Mr. James Littler, the choirma:ter. A capital dinner and tea were pnwided for the 24 boys of which the company consisted, and the day's programme included a drive round Little Orme's ,Head. • A most happy day was spent. If you want a lucky wedding ring go io 51, Hiaw-sr.,where you will get a present with it .—A dvt. A WIDNES MARINE STORE DEALER AND HIS WEIGHTS. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Frederick Bibby, of Hough Green, a marine store dealer and sail maker carrying on business at three establishments at Widnes was charged tinder six informations by Inspec- tor Kilpatrick with /raving unjust weights and scales. In the three places there were 36 weights, varying from lib. 3 ounces and 12 drachms light to 4 drachms light. There were also five weights which were too heavy, two fifty-sixes h. big over Sibs. too heavy, while a 281 b. weight was 41bS. 4i ounces too heavy. Thirteen weights were unstamped. There was also an unstatnped scale I which was 3lhs. 4 ounces out of balance. The Inspector pointed out that the defendant bought and sold goods on his premises.—For the defence Mr. F. .1. Poole, solicitor, said Mr. Bibby's business consisted principally in buying • old rope and cable, which he disposed of to wholesale merchants, and it was weighed by the railway people or the dock people, and did not pass over his scales. A the place where the heavy weights were found very little business was done, and it was often closed. The defendant was fined £1 and costs in two cases and ! ordered to pay costs in the others ; total £4 14s.

4 -.THE TRAFFIC AT SALT PORT. At the newly-named place of import and export at the Weaver Pool of the Ship Canal, Salt Port, traffic has been very brisk during the past week, and it is satisfac- tory to note that tar. W. H. Smith, the master steve- dore has been fully able to cope with the demands made upon his resources, Since Saturday last the steam ship Coral has been discharged of 550 tons of cement and the Princess Sophia has been loaded with 500 tons, the St. Fergus 400 tons, Eastham 700 tons, Vell Park 700 tons, and the Celeste 800, the whole of these cargoes being salt. The total amount of salt loaded during the week has been 3,100 tons. There has also been dealt with a considerable amount of Bridgewater Canal traffic. There ! are at present at work at Salt Port three cranes on the new jetty, three cranes on the temporary jetty, and four flat derricks. Mere have also recently been dis-, charged at Salt Port, seven Sot loads of Walmet baulks which have been rafted, and are now stored in what is termed the " dead-end "of the -canal. There are stored between 300 and 400 of these baulks and a t,.tal of 700 are expected, all to the order of a Manchester timber merchant named Mr. J. Kirkham. Next week the S.S. A.W. Cafeman is expected with 800 tons of timber which will also be rafted, and stored. The above facts give some idea of the importance of the work carried on in this part of the Ship Canal. Both PRITCHARD'S Shops are under personal supervision .aid customers may rely upon recelvingevery attention,—Adrt. DUTTON BOARD SCHOOL.

The drawing examination of this school has been I recently held by Major Telford, M.M. local inspector,' and the report which is to hand states that the school, has been classed "good." The Governmentexamina- ' tion was held on the 9tlf June, and the grant earned •is £Bl 7s. 6d., which is £7 3s. more than last year. The average attendance for the year was 57. The school was &dared free in September last and the fee grant amounts to £l9.—The annual excursion in connection with the school took Mice on Friday last week, when 120 children and adults had a trip to B.outhport. They were accompanied by Mr. Sydney Stokes, the head- master, and Mrs. stokes. For the accornodation of the excursionists special carriages were attached to the nine a.m. train at Preston Brook, and Southport was reached at noon, a breakdown of the engine at Warrington causing nearly an hour's delay at that place. An ex- cellent dinner was immediately partaken of at the Temperance Institute, kept by Mr. Gresswell. The afternoon was merrily spent by the young' PeniiiP in donkey rides, swinging,a sail on the electric launch, and , other amusements. At half-past five tea was provided at the Temperance Institute, after which a start was made for home. Through the kindness of Mr. Shaw,the Carlisle express was stopped at Preston Brook, where the excursionists were set down at a quarter to nine. All expressed themselves highly delighted with the day's outing, and three cheers were given for Mr. stokes, before they separated. The cost of the trip was sub- scribed by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Sir Richard Brooke, Sir Watkin Wynn, Messrs. J. F. Brunner, M.P., H. Talbot, J.P., G. Woiteley, W. C. Jones (Oaklands), Mrs. Jones (the Elms), J. Chorlton Parr, R. W. Cox, Miss Milner, Dr. Carruthers, the Rev. Canon Heron, and others. JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, HlO- - axd 4, Bridge.st., Runcorn.--Advt.

Referring to the need for a judicial inquiry, "The Leader' says :—" Cases, scandalous in number as they are shameless in kind, have been brought to our know- lvdge, and we speak with the utmost respect for the meaning of words when we say that there has been at work on behalf of the Tory party, during the late elections, a widesprvad, an unblushing, and a well arranged system of bribery and cor- ruption. The system has been worked by means of the two well-known instruments—strong drink and ready-money. We mean plainly,' it says 'that colossal sums of money have been distri- buted by the Tories deliberately, and in some cases openly, as bribes to buy men's votes."

SHIP CANAL ACCIDENT. On Tuesday morning a labourer, named Foster, employed on,the Latchford section of the Ship Canal, was run over by a waggon and had his leg badly crushed. Ile was taken :to the hospital, where it was found that happily no bones were broken. He is doingilavourably. GALLANT RESCUE FROM DROWNING AT RUN- CORN. On Monday afternoon a boy named Thos. Potter, of Portland-st., whilst playing near Bridgewater House, fell into one of the locks. Martin Gilligan, of Cooper-st., who was passing, pluckily jumped into the water without waiting to remove any of his clothing, and rescued the boy, who was alters wards taken home. Gilligan was highly compli- mented for his gallant deed. A BOLD FARMER AND HIS LOCOMOTIVE. Mr. J. R. Whalley, farmer, Mill Green Farm, Bold, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, to answer a charge of allowing a traction engine of which he was the owner to be used on the highway without a license, and also for allow- ing the engine to be driven along St. Helens-road without having sufficient men in charge. A fine of 20s. was imposed in each case.—James Prescott, the driver of the engine, was summoned for being withouta flag man at least 20 yards in front, and he was fined 108. and Coq& DEATH OF I BLACKPOOL CELEBRITY. One of the most important links which binds the Blackpool of the past with that of the present was broken, on Monday, by the death of" Gipsy Ned," originator of the South Shore encampment. This well-known personage, who was born in Lin- colnshire, and married at the old church, Liverpool, has just died at ninety-one years of age. He was a grinder in the cutlery trarle,which be left, ana took to fishing, his wife, "Gipsy Sarah," eighty years old, telling fortunes. Ned was widely respected. WARGRAVE CHUIICA. Since the paragraph which appeared in our last issue was written respecting the refusal by the Rev. li. J. Wadeson, curate in charge of Wargrave Church, of the living of Christ Church, Croft, Mr..: Wadeson has reconsidered the matter, and has now signified to Lord Derby his acceptance of the posi- tion.—The living of Croft has been rendered vacant by the resignation of the Rev. J. Richman, the rector, and Mr, Wadeson who was appointed to the curacy of Wargrare in June is to be congratulated upon his appointment as Rector of Croft.—Mr. Wadeson, who for the past three years has held the post oh Assistant Diocesan Inspector for the diocese of Liverpool. was in 1886 licensed by the Bishop of Liverpool to his first curacy, at St. Gabriel's, Toxteth Park, Liverpool. Fifteen months afterwards he acted as locum tenens for the vicar of Wilmslow in Cheshire.—After a stay of six weeks, he was appointed to the curacy of St. James's, Pool- stock, Wigan, where he remained four years, until hie acceptance of the curacy of Wargrave.—We understand he will not take up his duties at Croft lintil September. "WHRN Furgittns PALL OUT":. DlSltili3AscE IT BARLESTOWN. On Friday night a disturbance took place between a gentleman from Warrington and an Earlestown tradesrnan,which ended in the former being accom- modated with a night's lodging in the police cells. It appears Mr. Thomas Burton, of Liverpool-road, Warrington, bad been visiting Mr. Simon Hazleton, ,grocer,of Earlestown, on Friday last. In the course 'di the evening, some dispute arose between them, ending, after hot words, in Mr. Burton knocking Mr. Hazleton down in the lobby of his house. Mr. Burton was put out into the street, but continued to make a disturbance in front of the house in Market-st. Mr.llazleton appeared at an upper win- dow, and requested Mr. Burton to go away, be he refused, and indulged in abusive language. The police were sent for, and P.C.'s Cameron and Cata- nach requested Mr. Burton to desist and go away, but he blankly refused to eo either, and he was ac- cOrdingly locked up. He was brought before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, at the Town Hall, Newton, on Satur- day morning, on a charge of being drunk and disor- derly, and was fined ss.and costs,which was at once paid. LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE RAILWAY. At a meeting of the directors of the above com- pany, held on Monday, it was decided to recom- mend the proprietors to declare a dividend for the past half year at the rate of 31 per cent, per annum, carrying forward a balance of about £20,000.

THE HARVEST. The farmers in this district have been exceedingly busy during the last few days of sunshine in gathering in their hay. The crop Is a good one generally, and they. say the season could scarcely have been a better one for wheat and oats, if they can only now be favoured with a few weeks' sun- shine. The corn has grown to its full size, and is gradually ripening. , CARPETS and Larfor.Euma made and fitted free of charge during stie at'. and W. DUTTOIkr'S Sankey-et.. Warrington. ACTIVITY IN THE CHESHIRE SALT TRADE. Those interested in the great salt industry of .Cheshire will be gratified to learn that its activity is now greater than has been the case for a consid- erable time past. More pans are working than at any period during the past year, and an additional numbet will shortly be started. This briskness is expected to continue throughout the ensuing year. The consumption of fuel is enormous, about 700,000 tons being used annually.

HOUSEHOLD LINENS hemmed and marked free of charge during sale at J. and W. DUTTON'S, Sankey-at., Warrington. SINGULAR FATALITY IN I COAL MINE. James Glover, of Golborne, a collier, met with a singular fatality on Tuesday. The deceased was employed at Edward Evans and Co.'s Edge-green Colliery,usually as a labourer, but owing to a know- ledge of horses was on Tuesday morning deputed to break in a new pony down the pit. Within a couple of hours he was found 600 yards from the pit shaft, between the pony and the first of a small train of coal boxes, in a sitting position, with a frightful gash in the head. The deceased presum- ably, had been either kicked or trodden upon by the animal. He was at once removed home, but died almost immediately afterwards. Deceased has left a wife and eight children.

Lord Crewe, of Crewe Hall, Cheshire, has written to a Crewe gentleman stating that his name was included in the list of Unionist peers through in- advertence. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDINT. That now the elections are over business appears very flat, through having returned to the old steady groove. We are no longer Liberals and Conserva- tives but fellow citizens dwelling together in good fellowship. That after the fatigue of the fight Mr. Brunner is having a few days' rest before commencing his Parliamentary duties. Mrs. Brunner and the rest of the family leave to-day for Pontresina, Switzer- land, where they will spend the month of August.

That, as previously, Mr. Brunner's address during the session will be 9, Ennismore Gardens, London, S.W., where Mr. T. E. Ellis, 51. P., may also be found. That the elevation of the Rev. div.head: PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT FARNWORT-11 GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
div.p: PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT FARNWORT-11 GRAMMAR SCHOOL.

The annual distribution of prizes in connection with Fernworth Grammar School was held on Thursday night in the large schoolroom. Mr. Enstace Carey presided, and there was n large attendance. In opening the proceedings, the chair- man alluded to the educational facilities afforded by the school, and urged the residents of the dis- trict to take advantage of them by sending tt eir sons in greater numbers. He commented in terms of praise upon the success achieved by the students during the past year. Mr. W. Harrison, 8.A., the head master said the most important event in the school work during the past year had been the examination for the certificates offered by the college of preceptors. Although the results the results this year were hardly equal to the phenomenal success of last year, when every student gained a certi- ficate, and all with one exception had been placed in the first division of the class for which they were entered ; yet there was sufficient evidence to prove that they had not been idle, for 16 out of 20 candidates had gained certificates. (Applause.) The certificates in the higher classes exempted the holders from the preliminary ex: amination in the Incorporated Law Society,the Pharma- ceutical Society, the Royal Veterinary College, the Insti- tute of Chattered Accountants, the Institute of Civil Engineers' and the examination for registration as a medical student ; and were, therefore, valuable, not only as affording entrance to these professions but as also indicating a high standard of general ability, (Hear, hear.) The following gained certificates : Class I. 'F. C. Riley and C. R. Lewis. Class 11. W. Denny, W., Nickson, S. G. Owens, !J. Swale, and J. Willistus. Class 111. F. E. Barlow, T. A. Rottomley, J. Edwardson, J. P. Hughes, E. L. Hunter, A. W. Lewis, J. T. Rollason, A. Sinclair, and G. D. Stead. Two students (F. C. Riley and .1. Williams) had gained cert. ficates from Mr. I. Pitman for proficiency in sliorthar. and had become members of the Phonetic Societe. He was glad to be able to record the success of two -former pupils of the school—Mr. A. E. Wareing had been suc- cessful in passing first in the honours grade in Fuel, winning a silver medal at the examination held in con- nection with the Liverpool School of Science and Tech- nology (applause) ; and Mr. J. Smith, of Farnworth, had successfully passed the matriculation examination of the University of London. With regard to the teaching staff there had been some changes, but although they had lost an old friend in Mr. Jones, yet they had been fortunate in securing as his successor Mr. A. C. Forsyth, M. A., a gentleman of scholarly attainments. (Applause.) The Chairman then distributed the prizes. The following were successful in gaining class prizes : —First class : Mathematics, C. It. Lewis ' • Science, F. C. Riley ; English, C. It. Lewis ; Latin and French, C. R. Lewis. Second class : Mathematics, J. Williams ; Science, J. Swale ; English, S. G. Owens ; Latin and French, W. Dickson. Third class : Mathematics, J. P. Hughes ; Science, T. A. Bottoinley ; Latin and Freneh, J. P. Hughes. Open Prizes : Good conduct, E. L. Hunter ; Drawing, J. P. Hughes Theory of music. F. C Riley ; Diligence in singing class (prize given by Mr. Forsyth) A. W. Lewis. During the evening a capital programme of music was gone through, the following taking part :—Messrs. Forsyth, S. G.' Owen, C. It. Lewis, A. W. Lewis, and W. A. Nicholls. The singing class also rendered several choruses in good style. Messrs. F. C. Riley and F. N. Mercer were the ac,com- panists.

AFfER. TILE NORTHWICH CONTEST.
CONSERVATIVES IN COUNCIL. ME CONSOLATIONS OF DEFEAT.

A special meeting of the Erecutive Committee of the North wich Division Conservative Association and Unionist officials at the recent election was held at the Constitutional Club, Northwich, en Monday, "to discuss matters connected with the election, and arrangements for the ensuing registration of voters." •

Mr. Ward (the chairman of the committee) presided, and said Mr. Brunner, in one of his speeches after the election, was reported to have said : ''lf I had been I ready to make a corrupt bargain to prevent the fight I could have done. It was promised me that if there was not a contest in the Knutsford Division I should not have one, but that is not the way I fight." He (Mr. Ward) could only say that no one had any authority to say anything to Mr. Brunner, or to promise him anything Nobody did anything of the kind. Mr. Brunner knew all the officials of the association who had power to speak. If Mr. Brunner chose to take the word of any- one outside, and to say it in public as if it had been an official intimation, they could not be held responsible ; but they could bear him (the chairman) out when he said that the idea conveyed in Mr. Brunner's remarks never entered their heads, and that their intention from the beginning had been to fight Mr. Brunner. (Applause.) He moved the following resolution : " That the Secre- tary be instructed to write to Mr. Brunner, asking for his authority for such a statement." Mr. J. Newell, in seconding the resolution, said lie had been pretty intimate with the business of the asso- ciation, and he was quite sure that Mr. Brunner was not justified in the slightest degree in making the statement lie bad made. (Applause.) The proposition was put to the meeting, and carried ' unanimously. ' The Chairman then said they had to consider whether, under the circumstances that had taken plzce, the beat- ing they had got, after the fight they had made, and the candidate that they had, who was second to none in the Country, they would contest the seat at the next election. Mr. Whiteley had don, his work so thoroughly and se well, and he lived in the hearts of the people, and many , kindly feelings were expressed all round, and he (Mr. Ward) would like to find another candidate like him. (Applause.) He hoped if they fought again, Mr. Whiteley would see his way to come and light with them and for them. (Applause.) Some of the districts had done well, but they knew others which had done much worse than formerly, although he did not think that they had been leayened by the great number of new voters in the new cottages built all round the district, and in which Brunner workmen had been planted. Some of the bad places were better than they were before, arid he would con- gratulate both Winsford and Runcorn as being decidedly better than they were at the last election. (Applause.) lf they went on improving on the line they had com- menced, he was perfectly sure that those two places would wipe off any majority Mr. Brunner might make in other parts. (Applause.) He proposed that "The best thanks of the Unionist party in the Northwich Division be and hereby are tendered to Mr. George Whiteley for the splendid manner in which he has contested the divi- sion, and for his consistent, straightforward, courteous. and manly conduct throughout the election." (Applause.) - Mr. J. EL Cooke said, speaking on behalf of the Liberal Unionists, he had the greatest pleasure in seconding the resolution. It would really he, to his mind, impossible to get a better candidate than Mr. Whiteley, for there wis,nq man- who had devoted more time, or benn more patient. His gc.od wife, too, had exerted herself for the goricl of the cause in every possible way. (Applause.) Mr. A. Hamby Lewis supported the resolution. He said he could not but admit that he Was considerably disappointed at the la,rge majority \obtained by Mr.' Brunner,lor he did I4e,that, if. they could not wipe ()Obis last majority erftiiely, they Might at ' any rate, have Yedtitecl it to the extent of 500 or 600 voter. There was Very little &Stith that the last week OH very heavily% againstthem: Men liked tti be on-the winning side, and when they saw that the this was set towards a GladAonian ministry, many weak-b-aCked ones lefttbam and went over to the Liberals. He added that Mr. Brunner talked about havihg defeated the party of coercion, but there was little doubt that the party of coercion was really and actually'Lltitennted by the Manager of Wilmington Works, •L"; a! - The resolution was then- put to 'The meeting, and carried unanimously and with acbiamatiOn. Mr. Whitefey said he did not think that since he had entered the division he had had such a painful task to perform as replying to the vote of thanks they had so kindly passed, and, as his feelings and emctions were somewhat strong, his words would he in inverse pro- portion to those feelings. He could only say this—had they been able to foresee 'the future five months ago, When be had the honour of meeting all the members of I the Club and many 'of the Unionist workers In the divi- grin for the first time in that room, he did not think any would wish to withdraw either one word or etion they had said or done since that time. (Ap- plause.) They had had a. very hard,fight, and he thought they had not in any way disgraced them- eves. (Hear, hear.) He believed the causes of their _eat were certainly what Mr. Ward had described— Wit the Liberals had a very much stronger voting strength down at Winnington works than they pre- viously had, and that, coupled with the la' ness of the election, unfortunately caused Mr. Brunner's majority to be greater than they expected it to be. That was no reason why, having put their hands to the plough, they Should now look back. (ApplaUse.) They must all be in one frame of mind, that the division must be fought on teireiy occasion an 'election' took place;and he WAS sure by hard work and continuous pegging away, if he Might use that expression; they would be thole to return, in the end, a Unionist representative for the division. (Applause.) Whether he fought the "division at any ensuing election, or whether any other gentleman fought it, he placed himself entirely at their disposal. (Loud applause.) He would indeed only be toceliappy on any future occasion t o come down to any meetings or any gatherings to make speeches or support the cause on any available occasion when desired so to do. div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
AT NV A4tRINGTON.

--- When a Parliamentary election comes round there are always a few ratepayers to be found who, through their own negligence, find they are not on the list. They do not take the trouble to put in an appearance when objected to, and are therefore struck off. In some cases objection is taken in con- sequence of errors of description, and these should be corrected. The new lists of voters will be on all church doors in Warrington, on Monday next, and I strongly advise Liberal householders to see the lists and if tney are left off, or find any errors, let them see Mr. Clayton the Liberal agent, at the Liberal Club. Claims to be placed upon the list can be made up to the 20th August. I cannot help being struck with the contrast between the remarks of Gipsy Smitn in America in his lecture last week on that country and those of the Rev. Father Munell some months ago in War- rington on the same subject. The rev. gentleman probably did not find himself so much an idol in America as he has done among his admirers in England, hence his somewhat indiscriminate on- slaught upon the country. Gipsy Smith, however, characterised the Americans as a splendid people, and generally eulogised them, in a manner which. I think they deserved. Certainly the Americans have of late been developing deplorable characer- istics which I touched ill )11 last week, and which are a great stain upon their reputation. But the manifestation of these has been in tire less civilised parts of the country where the law is most inopera- tive ; arid I am much afraid that if the same civil conditions prevailed in England we should in time have the like appalling outbreaks of savage lawlessness. The faults of the Americans are the faults of human nature" when let loose from . restraint ; and not those of Americanism particu- larly. The conception of the American as a tall bony

, Yankee, witti cheroot and sombrero, blustering and exp-ctorating continually and "calculating" un- ceasingly that he could lick the Britishers and the" hull tarnation universe" is a ridiculous and ' senseless caricature, as wide of truth as the poles , are asunder, And yet people who pride themselves I upon their common-sense and realistic practicality will persist in thinking of the average American in this childish and foolish way, with the result that when any of them chances to cross the Atlantic to look at these supposed eccentric beings his, travel thitherb-coines to him an education indeed. Dickens who, d _Ate his genius, seemed to live in an everlasting grin at everybody and everything went to America; ,and instead of correcting the absurd impressions of bis ,countrymen, sacrificed truth to his love of the grotesque, and only con- firmed their silly prejudices. The fact is both Jonathan and John Ball as they are depicted are the veriest myths, and ought to be relegated to the limbo of all old-world foolishness. : tas

was, ple%sed to read' the accatut Of.,the view of the " Arab:Auer" representative with the Vicar of St. James,, Latchford, as to the proposal., that the Corporation should purchase old St..himes'is 0 burial gtound and convert it into a place of public.: recreation. I fervently hope this idea will be car-1 ried out. In work-a-day Warrington such placee are pre-eminently necessary, and with all due flefe-*: retie:" to the authoritits and due regard for the park'. I-ivOuld venture to say that it is far from being se; paradisacal a place as it might be. The proximiti." of smoking manufsctories makes it almOst, the la 4" place to go to seek &breath of really unpolluted and eee a bit of 'bluisky. It is a pleasant place to, , pass an hour in, but I think, all things considered.? ' that an open recreation ground at Latchford end, out of the smoke, would not be a superfluous thing for the inhabitants of the other side of.the Water. • London is being-gradtially made a perfect ram in tzibe by the aeivisitibn Of 'disused burial grounds, and other piecestif land 'for recreational purposes • 'td I haveyead that a Clergyman at Bethel Green whose churchyard had been so utilised turned its Ponversion to account in an ingenious way. He had the ciburtli wall behind. the pulpit opened so that he could overlook the churchyard, and after the usual evening service in the summer, delivered. another discourse to the pleasure seekers outside. I think that the utilisation of the ground at Latch- ford for recreational purposes would be not a dese- cration but a cons .cration of it. To give pure happiness to human beings is a nobler work than any consecration service.

I see the Rev. F. Slater mentioned that sheep had been put into the ground to keep the grass down. This reminds me that I once happened to be in .a country town at a time when there was quite an agitation going on among its community through someone having publicly pointed out that sheep were grazed in the churchyard, and that, as they were cropping the rich grass manared by human remains, they were really converting defunct Citiv. ens into mutton, and those who ate this mutton'. were a mild species of cannibals. The parson of the , place tried tried to make it appear that there was a beautiful and piously emblematic significance in sheep grazing in the churchyard, but the inhabit- ants would not have it, and the sheep had to go. The community were set at rest, they breathed freely to think they were now released from the haunting fear of cannibalism.

But lo ! a tormenting scribe in the local press presently pointed out that though the sheep had gone, the churchyard grass was converted into hay, and this was eaten by cows which supplied milk tor the inhabitants, therefore he maintained that the only change that had been made was that they were drinking instead of eating their defunct an- cestors. Some people, I fancy, got into. it ha fever over this, but whether the haymaking was stopped to dispel the alarms of these cr441:8, I don't know.

I boPe none of my readers will take 'fright about the sheep in the Latchford old burial ground, and think they will be swallowing old Latchfordsans. Zven the last tanner buried there—and Shakes- peare's gravedigsrer in' Hamlet" say tanners hides *wear the hardest below ground—will have tong since mingled with the elements; and the mutton pro- duced on the spot will have no deaa ancestor in it. But I hope the place will soon he used as a plea- sure ground for other than sheep.

CHARGE OF POCKET PICKING AT THE FAIR.

Thomas Troy, who lives with his mother in Berry's Yard, Tanner's-lane, a youth who is deaf and terribly marked about the face, apparently from erysipelas, was charged at the Warrington borough police court on Monday, with picking the pocket of Sarah Ann Lawton, of 23 Orford-lane, on the fair ground, about a quarter to nine on Saturday night, of a purse containing 9d. and a "lucky bone." He was also charged with trequenting the fair ground with felonious intent. It appeared that William Metcalf, of Mersey-at., and Thomas Dsrkin, of , lewsey-road, saw the prisoner with his hand in a' woman's pocket, she walking away unconscious of what had happer.ed. They laid hands on him and took from him the purse in question, but the woman got out of their sight. He resisted them strongly, but he was taken into custody, on the second charge. The prose- cutrix on Sunday morning came to the police station, and described correctly her purse except that she said there was about 9.1. in it, and the money in it was only 511. The prisoner was sent to gaol for 3 montha with hard labour.—Thomas Usher, 9, Morris's. court, was charged with stealing from Ellen Smith, widow, 9, Jolley-st., on Saturday night, a purse contain- sag 153. 31. The complainant felt a pull at her pocket, and put her hand out behind and caught the thief, but los got away with her purse. The Chief Constable said the complainant had identified the prisoner, who was apprehended by P.C. Bayendale while passing the Police Station, the officer having gone out to disperse a crowd opposite. During the time that the woman was lodging her complaint 2s. I4d. was found upon him. The com- plainant now said she had not seen the face of the thief when she caught him, and she gave the crowd's des- cription of him to the police ; and the prisoner was dis- missed, the Mayor,however, remarking that he had been too often at that court. CHARGE Or STEALING A SHAWL.

James Pickett,was charged at the Warrington borough police court on Wednesday morning, with stealing a shawl the property ot Annie Daley, Naylor-street, with whom he had been living. The Chief Constable saidthe complainant, the prisoner, and five others, were drink- ing in Mullins's beerhouse and their money being done, ' the defendant snatched the shawl, a new one, from Daisy's shltullers to dispose of it that they might get more drink. She objected to his having it, saying he had got one from her the previous day, an I she had given 24. for the new one, but he ran off with off it.— The complainant was not now disposed to proceed with the charge, though, on being pressed, she admitted that the prisoner took the shawl without her permission.— The case was dismissed.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednes- day,Thomas Isherwood, plumber, a married man, of 90, Pierpoint-st., was charged with stealing from the moulders' shop at Dallam Forge, between 6 p.m. on the 21st, and 6 a.m. on the 22nd inst.. a quantity of tools, value 34. 64., the property of Tames Warhrick, William Rowlands; and Thomas Watmough. The Chief Con- stable and the witnesses stated that the prisoner went to Mrs. Leslie's shop in Mersey-st., on the 22nd inst., and sold her the tools for is. 3d., representing that bp was IL moulder's master, and he came again 011 'Monday but she having been informed by the police that had been stolen, gave I im into the custody of a man in plain clothes, who was at the door, ant. in and heard him say a Yorkshireman had given the tools. The Chief Constable said that although ' point-st. abutted on D dlam Forgo, he did not know where it was The prisoner pleaded not guilty, and :aid he never stole or sold the tools, but it was a mallet and another article he took to Leslie's.—lle was sent to prison for 14 days with hard labour.
