TOOK THEIR HOLIDAYS. The followinz case was heard at yesterdays' Borough PoHas Court:—Ellen Yakes,an apprentice fustian cutter, left her work on the sth July, and had since been danc- ing in the park and enjoying herself. Her employer,Mrs. Mary Ann Travis, was granted an order for her return to work, and costs for the loss of time.—Sirah Ann Fairhurst and Mary Yates, apprentices to Mr. John Bolton, al,lo left their work on the same date for an unauthorized holiday. They were ordered to return to work and pay costs. SHE FINDS MARRIAGE A FAILURE.

Sorrow was expressed amongst the spectators at I Warrington Borough Police Court yesterday, for Mrs. I Ellen Johnson, of Bostock-st. She had her husband up for assaulting her on Sunday night. Amidst fast falling tears I she said he was her third t• man." She had tried to in- duce the other two to be good by bringing them into court. But she couldn't. When she entered wedlock, with William, the third one, she was consoled by the saying that" the third time does for all." But even that had turned out a fraud like all other unauthorized pro- verbs. Instead of being kind, and cooing, and gentle, he boxed her ears and sold her furniture, and put her in the back yard with the cats and the rain. He often did .4 before Sunday night • and once he pawned his army medal, and when she did it last week but one he aid what she told the Bench. " I'm tired, and weary of the cruel world." she said "It's so hard-hoo-hoo-oo."--" You will pay ten shillings costs William, and be bound oveq to keep the peace for six months," said Alderman Llarriso n.

As SITE WANT FOR STIPPEIR BRET/. The following circumstances transpired at yester- day's Warrington Borough Police Court :—Esther Wilson is a young married woman living in Robson- street. She was charged with having assaulted Mrs. gate Warren, of the game street, on the Bth of July. Mrs. Warren, who had art imp .diment in her speech .lisped a tale to the following effect : On Walking Day Mrs. Wilson threw a glass at her husband in the Prince of Wales' beerhouse. The glass broke—not on her hus- band's head—but on the floor. So exasperated was Mrs. I Wilson at haying to pay for it that she met Mrs. Warren outside and firmly but unkindly knooked her down on I her hack in the mud. List Tuesday afternoon Mrs. Warren was talking to a neighbour over the wall. When her false teeth fell out of her mouth she looked loony. Her neighbour laughed, but Mrs. Wilson said "go inside I and don't pull your ugly mug at me." Mrs. Warren picked her teeth from the garden, and put them in her mouth, and said" shut up.' Mrs. Wilson Towed yen- gance ; and when her so-called enemy was going for .supper beer that night she met her, knocked the jug out of her han: and then tried to knock the false teeth down her throat. Mrs. Wilson could offer no defence, -and was bound over for six months in a surety of £5.

A NEIGHBOURS' FEUD Possessing some exciting propensities occurred in EBEL?Id-st., on Saturday evening. Mrs. Alice Dauthy was 'aggrieved person. The previous week, she said, her next door neighbour, Mrs. Lawrence Spencer, had ileveloped a perversity for banging her (Mrs. Daulby's) grandchildren with clogs and other handy articles. She got Mr.. Arthur Browne solicitor, to write a letter to , Mrs. Spencer, demanding an apology. By last Satur- day night no apology had arrived, but Mr. Spencet Fad, and he was in a state of exhilaration which Mrs. Daulby termed " toddy." When she left her backyard to go for something for supper at ten o'clock Mr.

Spencer followed her. He brought to bear upon her the whole of his swearing vocabulary, and not being possessed of a Knight errant's courage she began to beat a retreat. Then, she said, he rushed into his yard, seized a prop, clambered on to the wall, and frantically probing the prop at her, com- menced to yell : " Yah ! you (hic) blessed old shod—(hic)—yer grissley, greyheaded (hic) 01l she cat. Lemma ger at yer—(hic)—l'll scalp yer ; I'll kill yer (hic) ; I'll rock (hic) yer into squashed Clam. Then she said he bsed language so foul that she dare not repeat it. Crowds of neighbours swarmed around the walls and gates to watch the fun, and then she sent for a policeman.—Lawrence Spencer told quite a different tale. He said Mrs. Daulby came into his back yard and exasperated him by alluding to an occasion, two years ago, when he rather foolishly belaboured his better half with the fire irons. She said to him : "Now, then, have you got the poker again ;" and he merely ordered her out He didn't want to cut her held off or anything like it. He merely put her out of the yard; and he never used any foul language, nor the threats for which he was summoned.—Mrs. Dalby's husband said Mr. Spencer must be a bad man. He never spoke a word to him in his life, but he remem- bered once having a drink with him. Mr. Spencer swore at his wife on Saturday, and threatened to cut her head off. He further insulted him by saying that he was fall- ing to pieces, which was untrue because he was only 60 and could easily walk. He admitted having called Mr. Spencer a thief ; but his own sons often called him that and threw clogs at him.—lt took an hour to hear the case. Mr. A. Browne (for the complainant) and Mr. P. Davies (for the defendant) tried to settle the matter amicably several times, but their clients would'nt agree. Eventually the Bench dismissed the case, the parties having to pay the casts between them.

CHARGE OF STEALING A WHIP.-Wm. Brown, Lord Nelson-street, and John Haines, Lythgoes-lane, were charged with stealing, on the 21st inst., from a trap while it was standing near the Cheshire Lines Good Station, a driving whip the property of James Lashford, butcher, 104 Orford-lane. It appeared that the com- plainant's sea drove to the station in the trap to meet his father, and noticed the defendants hanging about with a donkey cart. He went into the station, and when he came back the whip and the prisoners had gone. The complainant on the afternoon of the Mid saw Brown in Bank-street, and asked him about the whip, and he denied all knowledge of it. The police were in- formed and Detective-sergeant Monaghan discovered the whip in Brown's possession. Both the men pleaded guilty, but were dismissed with a caution. Mosney.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) and

; Alderman Harrison. DRUNK AND ASSAULTING A CONSTABLE. George O'Hare was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart in Sankey-st., on Saturday night, also with assaulting P.C. A. Hollinworth. On being apprehended by him on the first charge, he struck the constable violently, and he had to get the assistance of P.C. Clough to bring him to the station. He was fined 20s. DRUNK AND DISORDELLLY.—AN EPIDEMIC OF RU E- FIANISIC—WiIIiam Cunningham was charged with being drunk and disorderly and breaking a window at the Blue Back Inn, Allen-st., doing 2s. 6d. worth of damage.—The landlord said after serving the defendant with drink, he found he was drunk and took it away and put him out,upon which he returned and smashed the window.— He was fined 55., and the damage.—Joseph Renshaw, drunk and disorderly in the Market Place, on Saturday night, was fined ss.—William Cosgrove, in Morris's Court, on Sunday morning, ss. and costs.—Edward Burke, in Winwick-st., on Saturday night, ss. and costs. Frederick Hanson, was charged with baing drunk and disorderly on Planer's Brow, on Saturday night, also with assaulting P.C.'s Turner and Sankey. He was abusing a woman in a chip potato shop, and refused to go out and kicked Turner, then kicked and tripped Sankey and knocked him down and they had to get Sergeant Cheney to assist them.—The prismor said Sergeant Cheney cut his head with his staff.—A witness named White said the prisoner in the shop said he was master of it, and owned all the row of houses. He des- cribed the assaults on the police, but said neither of them struck the prisoner.—lnspector Spinks said the man was like a madman.—The prisoner said he was all through the Egyptian war, and was not right when he took drink.-10s. and costs. Alfred Titchett was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-st., on Saturday night. The prisoner accused P.C. 42 of striking him in the face three times, but it was stated that he made no complaint of this at the Police Station.—He was fined ss.—Michael Murray and Thomas Laff, drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street, on Saturday night, ss. and costs each.—Jarnee ana John Marsh were charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting Alfred Flampson, Samuel Heald land %Vm.liipkios,in Legh-at., on Saturday night.—Hamp- son said he was standing with the other prosecutors conversing at the corner of Legh-st., about a quarter past 11 p.m., and one of the defendants threw a stone which hit Heald in the back. He turned round for an explana- tion and got a blow. Witness remonstrated with them, and James Marsh knocked him down, and when he was getting up someone came and gave him another "do." He struck his assailant with his stick. He did not know the men.—Heald said James Marsh struck him in the eye and John struck him in the mouth. He did not know the men.—Hipkiss said he was knocked down, and John tupped him with his head. He never saw the prisoners before, and not a word was passed t 2 them before the assaults.—P.S. Smith said about a quarter to 12 on Saturday night he was called to the scene of the disturbance, and was surrounded by eight or nine per- sons complaining of having been assaulted in a similar manner to the three complainants. He went to the prisoners' houses, and knowing the character of James Marsh, took aid with him, and brought the men to the police station. James was at once identified by the complainants. They were then drunk.—Tames Marsh said he was struck with a stick by one of the complainants without provocation, and John told a similar tale pretending that his head was cut with the stick, but Inspector Spinks said there was no cut there. —James was sentenced to a month's and John to 14 days' imprisonment, both with hard labour.—Albert Finch, of 13ewsey-road, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Froghall-lane, and with assaulting two married women named Margaret Bradford and Margaret Cottarn, on Sunday night. It appeared that one of the men made a remark as the women were passing, and Mrs. Bradford went up to them and asked it they were referring to her, upon which they set upon both women and knocked them down, casing a lump in Mrs. Bradford's head the size of an egg. They were fined 404. and costs each.—Samuel Harper, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Sunday night and with assaulting Mary Jane Hoyles, in Allen-st. He came up behind her and assaulted her in a most un- seemly way, upon which she gave him a " clout " and told him she would not allow him to do that kind of thing to her.—He was fined 20s. and costs.—Patrick Burke drunk and disorderly in Buckley-st., on Sunday night, se. and costs.—Ellen Reddy, an Irishwoman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Pitt-st, on the 17th Inst. She first laughed and then cried in the box, and made a most voluble demonstration on leaving the court, after being fined ss. and costs, the Chief Constable re- marking that she had had a drop that morning.

'THEFT FROM A SLEEPING MAN.—James Ward and George Smith, men of no settled abode, were charged with having stolen at Appleton, on the 13th July, a pair of double calipers,two straight edges,two pairs of shoes, two pairs of trousers and a vest, value in all 275., the property of Samuel Robinson, blacksmith, Acton Grange.—Robinson stated that on the 12th inst. he left two bundles, one of which contained the articles men- tiened,at the Saracen's Head. Stockton Heath. He took them away on the day following, and lay down in a lane near the Saracen's Head, placing one bundle under his head, another by his side, and fell asleep. When he awoke the bundle which he had placed by his side was gone. The following day on looking into a second-hand shop in Mersey-st.,he saw two straight edges. He entered the shop and asked th 2 woman who sold her the articles. She replied " that man there," pointing to Smith. The prisoner then said " If you will come with me. I'll show you the man that gave them to me." They went toget- her as far as the brewery at Wilderspool, where the prisoner pointed out Ward, who was standing near. The latter, however, denied all knowledge of the articles. Witness then accompanied them to Warrington, but when they got near Bridge Foot, Smith decamped. Wit- ness gave Ward into the custody of a policeman.—John C. Dalton, manager at the Tower pawnshop, Bridge street, Warrington, stated that on the 14th inst. he took the boots produced into pledge for 2s. To the best of his knowledge, Ward was the man who pledged them, but he would not swear to this. He also offered the ' calipers and straight edges in pledge, but witness refused to take them.—Anale Baxter, second hand dealer. 48, Mersey-street, Warrington, stated that the prisone r came to her house on the 14th inst. and asked for Bd.for the calipers. Witness mid they would be of no use to. her, but Ward said they would do for cooking purposes (Laughter.) Thinking they would do for that purpose, witness gave the man 2d. for them.—Mary Leslie, old clothes dealer, Mersey-street, Warrington, said she purchased the straight edges of Smith. About an hour and a half later Smith came into the shop with a pair of boots. Whilst he was in, the prosecutor entered the shop, and said the straight edges and boots bonged to him.—Evidence as to the arrest of the prisoners having been given, Ward was sent to prison for three weeks, and Smith for 14 days. _ _

ASSAULT ON A CONSTABLE.—John Mitchell, Moss Bank- road, was charged with being drunk and assaulting P.C. Davie, and doing damage to his trousers to the extent of 9d. P.C. Davie stated that defendant was causing a disturbance in Ann-st., on Saturday night. When asked to give his name he refused to do so, and kicked him on the knee, bursting his trousers. Defendant was fined 2s 6d. and costs for drunkenness ; for the assault he was ordered to pay the costs, 8. 61, and 9d.for the damage, as well as 4s. costs,or in all 225. 3d.,0r 21 days in default. CHARGE OF ASSAULT ON A YOUNG WOMAN.—James Holden, Simms Cross, Widnes, appeared to answer a warrant which had been taken out against him last May, charging him with assaulting a young woman named Ann Jane Jones, a domestic servant, employed by Mr. R. Taylor, Farnworth.—Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the defendant, said he believed the com- plainant wished to withdraw the charge. Complainant who was a Welsh girl and could not speak English, was accompanied by an interpreter. On being asked by Mr. Lewin whether she could speak English complainant answered "not much."—As complainant seemed unwill- ing to go on with the case defendant was dismissed on paying the costs, 7s. 6 d.

Secretaries of Cricket Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

NORTON PRIORY V. EATON PARK.—Played at Eaton Park, on Saturday. Score :—Nurton Priory, 57 ; Eaton Park, 52. Y.M.C.A. Y. PARNWORTII C.E.T.S.—This match was played on Saturday afternoon at Farnworth, and resulted in a win for the Y.M.C.A., for whom J. J. Matthews and E. Fidler played a splendid innings the latter making a splendid drive clean out of the ground. Score ;—Farn- worth, 59; 79.

WALSER'S BREWERY IST V CREWE STATIOL—The above match was played on Saturday last at Warrington. Re- sult Brewery 54, Crewe Station 23. R. Geering (sub) for Crewe did good service with the bat. 10 runs.

LATCHFORD PRIMITIVE METHODISTS V. BASH QUAY JUNIORS.—This match was played on the ground of the latter, and ended in a win for the visitors. Brown did excellent work with the ball for the visitors, taking eight wickets for five runs. Appleton played best for the home team. Score :—Latchford 31, Bank Quay 6.

GRAPPENHALL ST. W ILFRID'S 2ND T. P. WALKER AND SONS 2ND.—This match was played at Grappenhall, on Saturday. The visitors, who batted first, were quickly dismissed for 18 runs, which total the home team soon passed, making 49 altogether, and thus winning the game by 31 tuns. GREENINGS' TURNERS AND FITTERS V. BRICK-ST.— Played on Monday and Tuesday evenings, the turners and fitters handling the willow first, and totalling 47, Woods being tcp scorer with 18 The home side could do nothing, with the bowling of Woods and Chadwick, the latter doing the hat trick, the whole side being dis- I missed for 18.

CADISHEAD AND IRLAM V. PATRICROFT (2ND ELEVEN).- 1 The return match of these teams was played on Satur- day at Cadishead, and resulted in a win for the home team. Cadishead won the toss, and sent in the visitors, who scored 42. G. Wrigley captured seven wickets for 13 runs. Cadishead,going in to bat.were disposed of for 48 runs, of which G. Wrigley made 20 and J. Daniels 14. Cadishead thus won by six runs. WARRINOTON T. WIGAN.—The Warringtonians met Wigan at Arpley on Saturday. A capital wicket had been prepared, and Wigan, winning the toss, were first represented by Messrs. Rennick and W. Wall, the trund- lers being Mr. S. M. Crosfield and Smith the new pro- fessional. Wall got the former away for a couple in his first over, but the professional got Rennick caught with the last ball of his first over. Disaster did not stay here, for the telegraph board had not been altered when W. Wall was bowled by the home captain. With H. Wall and McConnell associated, a better face was put on the game, and runs coming freely from Smith, a double change was tried at 32, Messrs. J. J. Crosfleld and R. Smith taking up the attack. The change at once worked,for McConnell played one back to J. J. Crosfield, and the catch was safely held. The retiring batsmen had hit hard for his 25, and his innings was the only re- deeming feature of his side. Thirty-four runs were on the board. and Macaulay helped Wall to put thirteen more runs on, when the latter was lbw, his contribution being nine. At 52, the home captain took the ball from R. Smith, and from this point the two cousins carried everything before them. G. Clark brought off a couple of catches, whilst Clark effected a smart one at the wickets. The venture closed for 64, and this sudden collapse was due to the splendid bow ling of J. J. Cros- field. His figures read :-9 overs, 3 maidens, 9 runs, 6 wickets ; whilst in his last three overs he took four wickets for no runs. The task set Warrington was apparently an easy one, and that a right opinion was formed was evident by the easy manner in which Messrs. S. M. Crosfield and R. Smith played the bowling. Short runs were the order, and 20 were sent

'ER, SATUR. . . ; up in quick time. Over-eagerness, however, brought about the dismissal of R. smith, for failing to respond to the first call of his captain, he was run out with the score at 23. Captain Manson was bowled first ball, whilst only seven runs had been added when G. Clarke played one tamely back to Rennick. J. J. Crosfield again played a prominent part for his side, and runs coming freely. Macaulay took urrthe ball at Goodwin's end. At 55 a separation was effected, for the home captain hit out at Rennick, and McConnell hit out at a fine running catch. Bell had but a brief stay, but Clarke stayed to make the winning hit, but the Wigan total had only been passed by five when the last corner had his wickets disturbed. With L. A. Voisey as J. J. Crosfield's partner runs were put on at a rapid pace, the new corner hitting out vigorously. At 98 Rennick got past Crosfield's defence, hie 27 being made without a chance. Voisey hit merrily away, and although Smith hit hard he failed to realise many runs. At 122 Voisey got his leg in front of a straight one from McConnell, who had just relieved Goodwin, and although his 33 was deciiedly lucky, his cricket suited the onlookers to a nicety. Williamson commenced his score by driving Rennick to the bQundary, whilst a wild shy by Mcaulay increased a couple into six. Flo soon put together 16', and Wallington failing to trouble the scorers, the innings closed for 139, Smith taking out his bat for five. Score :

div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
MISCRLLANEOU%

At the Tranmere Wanderers' Football Club Athletic Sports on Saturday,.a Warringtonian, J. Buxton, was the winner in the one mile bicycle handicap, in which there were 34 entries. The race was a fine one all the way, but Buxton maintained the laad, and won with a fair margin of safety. The time was 2tains. 49 3-ssecs. At the same sports Webster, of Warrington, who is now running under the Salford Harriers'banner, followed up his Belle Vue success by appropriating the quarter-mile hurdles. G. Wright, of Widnes was the winner in the one mile handicap, 27fentries.

At the pleasant annual festival on Saturday, in con- nection with the Davenhant Ftbrat and Horticultural Show in Davenham.Park, J. Fl. Fair,,of Warrington, (25> ran strongly in the Quarter-mile, inowhich he had Barker of Newcastle, Staff., for his nearest opponent. The Warrington Harriers were 'strongly represented in the Mile, the mOst fancied being J. Barlbw (130). He, how- ever, was well beaten by H. Barton,,of Hartford (140), in the last lap,seeing.which the lengthy Price (130) went after Barton, and running gamely caught the latter a few yards (min the post winning by a foot. H. W. Bellian, of Warrington,won the mile bicycle race. At the Oldham borough cricket and football club sports on the same date. J. Clark, of•Wilines, was the first in the mile race,. andJ. P. Rabbit, cf Warrington scored at the Wigan R.A.0.8. sports the same day, H. Green, of Warrington won in the 200 yards (maiden) race, and in the two miles bicycle (open.) W. Leatherbarrow another War- ringtonian was ascend. At the Isle of Man Exhibition sports, in the mile bicycle race,.M. Bailey, of St. Helens, came in second.

"The Free Critic" in the "-Athletic News" says of the eticket meeting at Old TraffOrd, last week-end : " The only inniegs which could rank as first-class was that of IL Smith, and, indeed, the result of the trial may be put down to the success of Smith as a batter, and possibly the discovery of two good bowlers in Oak- ley and Swallow. The Warrington amateur obtained 32 in the first innings, and 67! in the second, and both were displays af great merit and.ought to insure &fur- ther trial. lia is not like his namesake from Oldham, and believes in hitting bans that should be hit, but at the same time he possesses a sound defence."

Lancashire's defeat by Somerset was immensely popular with, the supporters of,the western shire, the re- sult being looked upon as a. slight revenge for the two thrashings Lancashire gave Somerset last year. When S. M. Crosfield won the toss he thought matters were pretty plain sailing, and that his men had only to goin to get runs., but somehow or other calculations. were upset. The fielding of the Somerset men was excellent, not a chance bring missed. S. M. .11. Woods's ball got up a trifle, and the Lancastrians, playing him rather gingerly, got caught. The spectators—being westerners —almost went off their heads to see the north country men come out. Forty-eight was certainly a miserable total, and when it Is remembered that out of those Smith made 23 (not out) the scoring was paltry in the extreme. The !-omerset men did not faro much better than the Lancastrians,, Briggs being in splendid form.

The Lancashire League furnished a curiosity on Saturday, inasmuch as only one of the five fixtures was brought to a definite conclusion. This was not the fault of the weather, but it was due to the fact that in each of the four unfinished eagagernonta the side that went in first made too many runs. Indeed, mos were un- usually plentiful, nearly all the bowlers having a bad titue of it.

Warrington displayed something like their proper form in their cricket engagement with Wigan on Satur- day. It was the first meetinc, of the clubs this season. : The visitors batted first, but 'the whole side were dis- missed in an hour and a half for 64. The chief scoreg was M'Connelll J. J. Crosfield took in nine overs sla wickets for nine runs. The game was never in doubt when Warrington took up the attack, and although three wickets were down for thirty runs, Messrs. S. M. and J. J. Crosfield added 25 runs before the Warrinfiton captain was dismissed for a valuable 25. Clark made the winning hit, Rnd the innings terminated for 139, Warrington winning an interesting game by 75 runs. A trial was. given ,to Smith, a new professional hailing from Northamptonshire, and a favourable opinion was formed.

W Pliam Williamson, aged sixty-eight years,.was, at the Liverpcel City Police Court, on Moinhay, again charged with the murder of his wife in Beresford-street on Tuesday last, and after some additional evidence had been Own, was co-omitted for trial. At Devon ASSiaeS, on Monday, a youn unmarried woman named Lancey, of Combo Martin, was found guilty of child murder ; but the jury being of opinion that she was of unsound mind when she committed the act, she was orcNrecl to be detained daring her Majesty's pleasure. At Bow-street Police Court on Monday, Thomas Neill, charged with the wilful murder of Matilda Clover, by the administration of strychnine, at Larnbeth-road, in Octo. ber last, was further remantled,

div.head: DEATH OF/ BISHOP GIISIMINTON.
div.p: DEATH OF/ BISHOP GIISIMINTON.

Claughton, late Bishop of St. Albans,. died at his residence, Danbury Palace, near Chelmsfbrd,rat eleven °Week on Monday morning. He was seized with paralysis on Friday, and on Sunday .prayers for his re- vcoery werec,ffered in the Chelmsford churches, He was conseious almost to the last. Dr. Claughtont celebrated his golden wedding only a month ago. He resigned the bishoprio of St. Albans in 1890, and Ize was-then pre. seated with his portrait by the clergy and laity of the diocese. Since that time he had passed,aquiet life at Danbury, and he had been driving aboutrthe neighbour- hood within the last fortnight. The • late bishop was born at flaydock Lodge, Lancashire, in 1208'. He was educated at Rugby and at Trinity College, Oxford, where he was successively Scholar' Fellow,.and Tutor. He tookthe Chancellor's prize for Latin,verse in 1828, the Newdigate prize for English verse inthe following year, and in 1931 the-Latin essay prize.. He gratuated in 13333 taking a first-class in classics. He was made Pnblic Examiner in 11138, and some sixtsen years later waa appointed Professor of Poetry. In the interval he had become Vicar of Kidderminster and Canon of Rochester. He ultimately became Bishop of Rochester, and retained the old see until its dPrision,.whrn he elected to become the first bishop of St. Albans. The Iliiihopwas married in 1842 to the sistercf the late Earl of Dudley, who, with several children, survives him. One of bis daughters is the Duchess of Atgyll. He was corniected with the family of which Colonel, W. J.. Legh of Lyme Hall, and Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., for the New- ton diwision, are members. He was very intimate with the district of Newton-/e-Willevvs and Earlestown,. and several times preached in the district, the- last occasion being during the services in connection with the cease- crationof Earlestowni Church. A portrait of the de- ceased prelate hangs inthe Havdock Read;Ta-,e, Room.

Mnrtin Finnen, labourer, was charged with hav- ing wounded John Jones,landlord of the Nag's Efea,d Inn, Farndon, with a knife, on the 13th Jttly. Prisoner, it appeared, was refused drink at the :Nag's Head, and describing himself as a Home Ruler and Fbnian (so Jones said) to the backbone, threatened to "do" for Jones. A struggle followeri,.during which prisoner took out a knife, by which Jbnes was stabbed in the hand. Jones fetched a stick and chased the prisoner up a lane,where another scuffle took place, prisoner stabbing Jones in the head. The jury found prisoner guilty of misdemeanour, and he was sentenced to six months hard labour.

div.head: REMARKABLE, GENTEsTARIAN.
div.p: A REMARKABLE, GENTEsTARIAN.

The age of a centenarian named Thomas Morgan. re- siding- on the Welsh hills at Cwmbran, has just been authenticated as 105. A year ago he lost his wife at the remarkable age of 104, and he subsequendy fell down- stai's and broke five ribs. Afterlong and careful medical treatment he fully recovered, and was enabled to record his,vote for the local member et Parliament at the recent elections. Re is still enabled to move about with free- dom', and hopes to see his 106th year.

TO a qniet cottage at the foot of one of the New. •"4, ranshire hills came Mrs. Field, with her corn rtakm, Cecil Brand, for the summer. It was very eelY there; that was why Mrs. Field liked it. Stryker, the landlady, with her grand.daugh- -7r,. Bessie, and one farm servant, were the only Oti:i.ee inmates of the cottage; and there was but 6etother house in sight, beyond on the slope of the b Mrs. Stryker had had summer boarders before, et none like these; so grand, yet so gentle; rich • e knew, from all signs, yet so simple in their es; real ladies, if ever there were any, she de- ...t,1_4(1 to Bessie, her only confidant. And Bessie, :40 had felt the charm of the ladies' gentle voices "id gracious words, eagerly assented. Mrs. Field wal no longer young, but beautiful tWit.ii a beauty that time had only ripened and per- ececl ; though the lovely face had deep shadows t ' Pon it that sorrow's cruel hand had graven there, rrl, her eyes had a far-away, wistful, yearning h°:`, as if seeking the lost happiness that had once hers. Her companion was a fair young girl, right and winsome, and light of heart; whose prett to 3' caressing ways alone seemed to have power th soothe and help her friend. For Mrs. :Ugh not ill, was worn almost to a shadow by °le secret, brooding, gnawing grief. ~/ler story was a very sad one. She had been a reat belle and beauty, and from among a host of ~'wers had chosen and married, when in her thirtieth ;eear, Charlton Penfield, a gentleman some ten a als her senior. It was a true "heart marriage," no wife ever looked forward to a brighter life an did Mabel Penfield when her proud husband e 70,• tall°4l her as mistress of his beautiful home. For fa "tie they were happy; as perfectly happy as it d,„.granted to mortals to be; till jealousy—that adful jealousy which is crueller than the grave— crept into their paradise and distroyed it. It would hard to tell how Charlton Penfield let this foe lter his heart and drive out the great love for his V° which reigned there. That she was true to every thought and word did not matter; he „74 sc. blinded by this creel passion that he hall ne rty for her, and one dreadful day he cursed her the destroyer of his honour and happiness, and tlj°ve her, a pure, sinless, loving woman, out into 0 e bitter world. She was not penniless, for her Iva fortune remained to her; and, too proud to the world, which once had courted and caressed ee how she suffered, she went aboard at once. l Five years passed—lonely, wretched years. She her husband truly yet in spite of all, and the key, of the past was alike a pleasure and a rain. f The world is not so wide but that friends and a`/Ties meet in time, no matter how far sundered; zed' in a chance meeting with some old-time latetiutl,l4ances, Mrs. Penfield learned at lasi that nusband was seeking her. Then began her restless wanderings; for vague fears stirred ' h't Ilcart, and made her dread that he should find b:r. She WWI not alone now. In London she had, rae interested in a young orphan girl, Cecil 2d, who had done some sewing for her; and, ',l),g her by birth and education far above the -"ma in which poverty had placed her, had ado th Pted her as her niece. She had never regretted act. Cecil had become as dear to her as a 1 ghter, and in all her wanderings had been her devoted attendant. Mrs. Penfield had ri-"PPed a portion of her name, and, as Mrs. Field, sleZned herself so secure from her husband that BL had dared to come back to her native land. r. knew not why be sought her; knew not if AIN after the lapse of these eight long, weary ;Zs, he did, indeed, still seek her. But the fear uncertainty remained. 0, I want rest I" she cried to Cecil. Th 820-en Cecil had diligently studied the papers, • seeing Mrs. Stryker's modest little advertise- answered it, and, all arrangements speedily aiTe.Pleted, had taken her Aunt Mabel to Brook- • it • th.,, There auntie dear 1" exclaimed Cecil, tri- ' antiy, the morning after their arrival, as she ttled Mrs. Field comfortably underneath one of ~„' great, shady, pine-trees. "Could you find a ,e f-,,!ttier place for your summer rest Just snuff up 14is fragrant, piny odour; it is better than all your o,4leines. Listen to the ripple of that silvery little ee-e4; it is so merry it fairly seems to laugh at the t nhearns that come stealing down through the jeees to admire themselves in its clear surface; and the, Yonder 1 the blue hills, with the deep shadows littaising each other over them 1 and here comes to„"e Beesie with a foaming goblet of fresh milk You. IT is indolence that exhausts, not action, in which there is life, health, and pleasure. The spirits may be exhausted and wearied by em- ployment, but they are utterly wasted by idleness.
Do to-day's duty, fight to-day's temptation, and do not weaken and distract yourself by looking forward to things which yoa see, and could not understand if you saw them.

Ix was sold of Hannah' More that when she was told a tale against another in her villag.e, her reply usually was, "Come, we will go and ask if that be true." The effect was something wonderful. The tale•bearet, taken aback would begin to say, "Well, perhaps, there might have been a mistake," and to beg that no notice might be taken of the matter. But no; the good lady would go there and then, taking the scandal-monger with her, to make inquiry and compare accounts. If all tale-bearers could be treated in this way how few tales would be told I

THE poet Cowper says that roestic happiness is the only bligs that has survived the Fall." The great Martin Luther said; speaking of marriage— " The utmost blessing that God can confer on a man is the possession or a good and pious •wife ; " and again he said, "To rise betimes and to marry young are what no man ever repents of doing." One old English poet pronounced a true marriage" a pattern of celestial peace," and another called it " heaven on earth."--:

UNTIE THE STRINGS. —Said a most successful merchant to a lad who was opening a parcel: "Young man, untie the strings.; do not cut them." It was the first remark that he had made to a new employe- It was the first lesson the lad had to learn, and it involted the principle of success or failure in his business career, Pointing to a well- dressed man behind the counter, the merchant said: "There is a man who always whips out his scissors and cuts the string of the packages in three or four' places. lie is a good salesman, but he will never be anything more. I presume lie lives from hand to mouth, and is more or less in debt. The trouble with him is that he was never taught to save. I told the boy just now to untie the strings, not so much for the value al the string as to teach him that everything is to be saved and nothing wasted. If the idea can be firmly impressed upon the mind of a beginner in life that nothing was made to be wasted, that things the most trivial have their uses, you have laid the, foundation of success."

A PRIZE MEDAL DESIGN.

Sir,—ln passing the Lion Hotel, Bridge-street, a few gays ago, I noticed with pleasure, that the prize medal. design in tiling of one of our local School of Art students, had been utilized in decorating a portion of the new entrance hall. It is a tine piece of artistic skill, and reflects the greatest credit, not only upon the designer but also upon the school, and its teachers. There is a defect, however, which I would like to point nut, and it is one which rather mars the appearance of the work. lly some unaccountabie oversight one of the top corner, tiles has, been placed upside down, thus causing the design to appear broken. This no doubt can easily be I rectified, and the beauty of the work restored. Trusting you will be able to find space for this short paragraph in your valuable paper, believe me, yours truly, _` " • ART STUDENT. - -

TNE PAYMENT OF M.P.'S Sirs—Considering the question of the payment of /Member? of Parliament has been exciting so muck dis- suasion mad interest in this district, the following Rent which 1 have cut from a London newspaper will not be unacceptable to your readers : "It has just been discovered that it is legal for mem- bers of Parliament to demand payment for their ser- vices. I hope Mr. Burns or Mr. Hardie will try the ex- periment successfully entered upon by Mr. King, the member for East Harwich, who, after the dissolution in 1881, presented a petition to the effect that the borough had not paid him his wages, though often re- quested to do so. The Lord Chancellor issued a writ compelling the borough to pay the wages. Since that time, so late as 1857, Lord Chancellor Campbell gave his opinion to the following effect : ' For this point of the people's charter—payment of wages—no new law is needed. I know no reason, in point of law, -why any member may nct now insist on payment of his wages. The ,question is too important to be Allowed to wait until the House of Commons feels disposed to pass a gene- ral law for the payment of members." According to the above, all the existing agitatioz . on the subject of the payment of members, is uneeceasary, as it is admissible under the present law, and far this assertion we have so high anauthority as that of a Lori, -Chancellor. ? t' I should certainly like to ,see some member of tile Liberal Or the Lahonr party put the question to a prac- tical testi by applying for remuneration fcr his services in the late Parliament.—Yours truly, • ANLI ITS . , -- RIJNCORX TOWN BA2+D. Bir,--1 are sorry to have apatti' to trouble you on tlie -subject Of the above-named band, but the unsatisfactory position of affairs, and thesilence of those most interested, impel me to bring the matter before the public notice. Over nine months have elapsed since an appeal Tf as first made to the peeple of Runcorn to aid in the re-con- struction of Runcorn Volunteer Band on a wider and a more popular basis, by subscribing in their generosify towards the purchase of a full set of silver-plated instru- ments. 'Collecting cards were spread broadcast through the town, collectors were set to work, and a magnificept draw offering prizes in value from £5O down to the: pro- verbial tin whistle was advertised. What is the resultof all this effort, and of this alluring draw ? And echo answers a Whet ? It would appear that this is the only answer we are 'likely tosget if the matter is left to those in &nth** ' Their policy appears to he one of "mum." But the subscribers are far from being sati,sfied with this condition of aff +its, and as one of them, and on their behalf, I would ask the following questions, and failing an answer other steps will have to be taken to ascertain how matters stand. What- amount of 'money has been , • raised by means of the collecting catds, and what amount has been paid in by the canvassers who were out with collecting books? :Who are the trustees of the fund and in whose name has the'money beert'paid • into the hank? Is there sufficient to buy the instruments required, and .if not what is to be done with the money ? Then there is the draw about which an explanations needed. About 7,000 tickets were issued, and it Wils announced that the names of the prize winners woh,b be masie known in March. Afterwards when that tis!ie came, we were told that as' the whole of the tickets had not been disposed of, the draw would be posponed untAl May. July has now come and gone and not a word has been heard as to the affair. Has it taken place andwtto are tha-lucky winners? If not, when may we ex- pect it ? The csinduct of the people who have the whole affair in hand is most, incomprehensible. That a very large amount was taken is a certain fact, but it would seem * that those who have provided it are not to be let into the A secret of how itilas bees disposed of. As to the Prize Draw,it is e direct breach of faith not to hafelteldlt" very long before this, anti loot only is the reputation of the band suffering), hut people are losing confidence in the whole concern from beginning to end. , The he.st, thing those most concerned can do is to make skill and complete dectsnition of the state of the accounts and to nubllstSa list ed the subscribers, and at the same. time to bring the draw to a conclusion. Otherwise it would ' appear tio rue thast the band will only drag ,ort a asleep, able existence fes.Nsne time to come, and then. deserted by its friends and supporters, there will he an end of the R'uneorn Town Band, and of its unfulfilled openair concerts and the manifold other services it was to ren- der to the town as repayment to a generous public, in accordance with promises made. Such a termination would be much to be deplored, and the officials by an open and straightforward policy may assert it. Will they do so? Yours, &c.
SUBSCRIBER.
Juty 28th, 1892.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
MORE MONEY WANTED.

Sir John Harwood on Thursday prasented a report to the Special Consultative Committee of the Manchester City Douncil embodying the views and observations of the Corporation's representatives upon the Board of the 'Manchester Ship Canal. The report contains a concise statement of the negotiations between the ' Ship Canal -Company and the Corporation in 1814, and of subse- quent procedure. Deep regret is expressed that the estim ates first presented by the company to the City Coucil and the measurements on which they vere based ;had proved so unreliable. Stress is also laid on the nn- •necessarily expensive character of so—e «f the materials -used in connection with the works. The Corporation directors du not anticipate that the canal will be open for tr,ffic to Manchester before the end of 1893. They estimate that the amount required in addition to the existing resources of the compa..y is, in round figures. a, million and a quarter,. and allowing; for reasonable contingencies, the sum is brought to a million and a ,half.

div.head: BREAKING A CYCLE RECORD
div.p: BREAKING A CYCLE RECORD
grai

The cycling record between Cheater and Man- •ehester—a distance of 40 miles—has just been broken by Mr. J. B. Johnson, a member ot the War- rington Cycle Chib, who rode a Burton rdiachine. Mr. Johnson started from Chester on Monday even- ing at 6-20, and rode the distance of 40 miles to Manchester, in 2 hrs. 22m.52secs, arriving in St. Ann's Square. Manchester, at Bh. 42m. 52 secs, thus completing the grand performance of breaking the record by 34 minutes. The rider was mounted up- -on a Burton chainless (70 inch geared) spring-frame Ssfety,and was paced from Chester to Mere by Mr. •It.H.Carlisle.Liverpool,and thence to Manchester by ,Mr. Newton of Winton, Manchester. The record was ( fficially timed by Mr. J. E. Berry Y.R.R.A., Congleton. Mr. Johnson encountered a pretty stiff wind during the greater part of tke ride, and his performance ia therefore all the more-creditable to him. It may be mentioned that' Mr. Berry who kept time took train to-Manchester after starting Mr. Johnson at Cheater, and reached St. Ann's Square &short time—and only a short time—before the rider completed his journey. The machine ridden will shortly be on view in Deansgate, Man- cheater, and afterwards in Warrington.
TFE' HOME RULE QUESTION.

- 1 it r . =To the Editor of the "Examiner.' Sir,—Although Sunday Closing, a point, the one point, on which some of us did not entirely agree even with the moditiod views of our Candidate, had perhaps more than anything else to do with our defeat at the recent election, I have not a shadow of doubt that want of proper information, and instruction on the Irish question contributed largely to that result. Twenty minutes canvass and the common-places of party speeches were not sufficient to ineet.the wide-spread error that still prevails. I know very well that the " Examiner has done yeoman service to the cause of Home Rule, and I think others who are in earnest should do their best to bring home to their friends the realities which , will guide, and to dissipate the illusions that mis- lead, them. "'Therefore I enclose you a copy of a ' letter whicil Lam sending to a friend of mine of pronounced Unionist Proclivities. I think the iacts therein quoted may help to expose the bugbears, and show up some of the hollow mockeries of mis- called Unionism, spread by every Tory leaflet, blazoned on every Tory poster, repeated in every Jingo harangue, by which, as on every former oc- casion, we recognise the effort to pervert English opinion and judgment on the Irish question.

Yours truly, A. H. CROSFIELD. :Warrington, July 291 h, 1892. COPY OF LETTER.' I am sorry to hear, that from a passive, you have become an active, opponent of Home Rule for Ire- land. You predict, so lam told, Civil War if we ant it; but why? You surely do not believe that the interests of Belfast and other commercial Centres in the North, would be jeopardised. Were there any evidence for this notion, should we have Ulster-men, Protestants, and Catholics alike, the whole of their property and fortunes bound up with Utster,;coming over to tight the battle of Home Rule, as many of them do? The chief apprehension of those who take the other view, is, so I was once informed by Mr. T. W. Russell, a graduated income- tax. rt is quite possible there are sonte grounds for this apprehension, htit they would be, to say, tie least, as likely to see an alteration in the' incidence of taxation under 'English as under Irish rule. Indeed, more is heard of a graduated income on this side of the channel than the other. Its adsneates say, that A with an income of £2oo'a year, ought to pay less than 13 with £2,000, and B than C with £20,000, the heaviest rate in th'e ..e'falling on D with £200,000. Others think t hat fajrlygraduated death duties would he still better; f hatwe should increase the amounts transferred at their deaths, from the fortunes of the richest members of the community, abolishing, of course, the anomaly that, at pre- sent exists in the extraordinary distinction between landed, and other property. Whatever coUrse may be finally taken, mat belief la that, sooner, or later, we shall see the adoption, of this principle in taxation, and I also believe that an honest attempt to readjust the burden of taxa- tion so that more of it may rest on the shoulders of those who, possessed of great wealth never, feel it, or fall upon their tortunate euccessors, -will not be in the end, prejudicial to the interests of either, but on the Contrary will help to guarantee more securely and permanently the right of the individual to amuse as:large a fortune as he can by his own pertiestrance, esirgy, and pluck, Absolute freedom, unlimited scope for the ambi- tion of iddividusj capitalists has been, and, of course‘ must remain Ear indispensable coddition 'of • our success in the great commercial struggle between; nations, but our position will not be the weaker but the stronger if the public revenues are increased by a fairer contribution from the great fortunes piled up under the state's protection. After national expenditure has been properly dealt 'with and the sinking fund, fog instance, secured, we shall be able to find good use for any surplus that remains, in assisting those projects, national or local, by which as time goes on the conditions of life are to be gradually improved for the great masses of our population, and opportunities for wider int6rests and healthier resources offered in proportion as there is developed more capacity and yrillingnest to grasp them. And so I think that Mr. Russell atul his friendsrnay make up their minds that some day or other, thereitreiU be a modilication of our present method of taxation ; but Radical reforms in that or anything else arem likely, or rather, perhaps, more likely to have their origin in Lancashire or Landon, than in Ulster or Munster. The fact is, that amongst the masses in Ireland, there has been far less independence, far more submissiveness, than amongst the working-dlasse§ of England. They are beginning to waken up in IrAnd, no doubt,but still the influence of birth and high station in any department of life is greater there nail with us. I am not specially condemning it; respect for high birth and high position in life, if nonsequent responsibi- lities and duties are honotnablrundertaken and per- formed,is surely derogatory•neither to those who pay,nor those who receive it. But in Ireland it has often ex- ceeded the bounds of legitimate respect. No' one who has mixed with the people at all cm have failed to have noticed that. It is chiefly the natural, and inevitable consequence of the conditions under whicir the agricul- tural portion of the country have lived, A condition up to comparatively recent times of practical serfdom. Can any one doubt that among such a people, the wealth and power of the northern Protestant centres will have their fill Share of influence in the national Parliament, and eqnally so the, representatives of capital, and the wealthier stmta of society from the other provinces— especially if the representation of the country is estab- lished on lines resembling these of the Bill of 1886? k I ventured to make these observations about the con- servatism of the Irish to a Unionist member for an Ulster coestitueacy the other flay. He endorsed them, and added that he disarrayed of the attempt to arouse fears of 'an armed rising in the Nora on' Home Rule being granted.

But it has been suggested that if the Counties of Down and Antrim won't have Home Rule, they might be excluded from any measure of it that may be pasieti. What is the answer ? So far as I hayo Been, the dnly answer was given by some leading Unionists in Belfast, Including, I believe, the celebrated Dr. Kane. And they declined to be left out! Does that argue any reality in their apprehensions? These Orangemen won't have .Home Rule themselves, but they refuse to allow us to grant it to the rest of Ireland without them! Here at last we are to have a perfect illustration of the " tail wagging the dog." The Leader of your party in the House of Commons lays great stress on the opposition of Narth East Ulster to Home Rule—though I am afraid he, and others do not usually take the trouble to distinguish between a a portion, and the whole of Ulster. Let us see what his opinion was a few years since. In 1884 he (Mr. Cham- berlain) spoke as follows at Newcastle What shall I say of the self-styled Loyalists, who, with fulsome pro- fessions ot their *devotion to the Crown, insult and defy the representatives of the Crown in Ireland, and who break the law themselves while they pretend to defend it? I believe at this moment, if there is any danger to ithe peace in Ireland, it lies in the proceedings of a certain section of the populatioa in Ulster, led by men of rank and by men of education, who know enough to know better." Now he turns round, and says the danger is the other way, lending himself to the Orangemen's cry, that their interests and liberties will be in danger if we grant Home Rule. Supposing Catholics did attempt to treat Protestants with bigotry, and intolerance; where would they be likely to begin? Not, at any rate, in the North. There are in Ulster 873,524 Protestants, and 744,353 Catholics. In other parts of Ireland, the Catholics out-number the Protestants in the proportion of 10 to 1,20 to 1, or it may be 100 to 1. Have you ever heard of Protestants, as such, being in anyway illtreated in these parts in all the exciting years of the last decade, when surely party feelings were likely to run higher than after the great question of Home Rule, which divides them has been settled? What are the tarts? In Cork nine Protestants were elected on the first city Council after the Irish compensation Bill ; and that mind you when the Protestants had been keenly resisting the gift of any open Municipal Corporations to Ireland. The first Mayor was a Catholic, the second a Protestant, and others have followed, one Protestant mayor having been elected three times. " In the case of Dublin, there have been 15 Protestant Lord Mayors elected in that Roman Catholic city (Roman Catholic by a considerable majority) since 1850. and many Protestant sheriffs. In Limerick, a Roman Catholic town, there have been 15 Protestant Mayors since 1843, and 12 Protestant Mayors in Waterford since 1845. But perhaps (as Mr. Gladstone says, in the speech from which 1 am quoting) " the best test of all is where there is a little money to be fingered. Compare the behaviour of the Catholics in Dublin, with the Orange- men in Belfast. In Dublin, the Nationalist Corporation have laid out on the remuneration of Civic officers about £8,400 a year. Of this £4,400 goes to Protestants, and £4,000 to Roman Catholics. Commentin,g on this,Mr.Glad- stone says," So far as I can make out,thelrishman is quite as little given to jobbing as the Englishman. Jobbing is not unknown in this country, and I think what I have shown you proves that the Irishman has no especial Gr undue inclination that way ; and as to prejudice be- tween Protestants and Roman Catholics, what he looks for is the best man, and he tries to appoint the best man to the office."

- - ponsibilty in the Government- of their country."- The following are • extracts from his speeches :—Glaegowil September 15th, 1885 :—" I have always thought that it, was one of the cardinal objects of Liberals to make the Union between the three kingdoms a union of feeling ' and affection as well as of law, and I have believed by such a union alone could the prosperity of the people be assured. I have desired to see a real co-operation be- tween the democracy of Great Britain and the National party in Ireland." So much for the jeers in Birmingham at the "Union of Hearts." June 17th, 1885, at Hollo- way :—" It is a national question as well as a parochial question, and the pacification of Ireland at this moment depends, I believe, on the concession to Ireland of the right to govern itself in the matter of its purely domestic business.-, , ' •. ' With him Home Utile is Only a question of ways and means---zoply one of his own schemes must be adopted. Other people; Mr. Gladstone included, are too clumsy in their attempts, lle is, of course, entitled to think so,but ' holding these opinions, he is not entitled to insinuate that we who see with himself that self-government is the ra- t. 1 tional solution of the Irish problem.are traitors and turn- coats because we do pot think him the most experienced and competent statesman we can find to carry it. "It is a national question as well as a parochial question, and the pacificatiOn of Ireland at this moment depends, I believe, on the concession to Ireland of the right to govern itself in the matter of its purely domestic. bust- ness." Bui this is all we contend for. A good deal of personal interest may attach to the question, whether Mr. Chamberlain has lately changed his opinions, but whether this may be so or not there are higher authori- ties to appeal to. "In no other history, says Mr. Lecky (referring to Ireland) can we trace more clearly the chain of causes. and effects, the influence of past legislation, ' noVonly open the material condition but also upon the , character of a nation. In no other history especially Oh we investigate more fully the evil consequences Which must ensue from disregarding that sentiment of nationality which,whether it be wise or foolish, whether it be desirable or the reverse, is at least one of the strong- est and most enduring of human passions. This, as I • conceive, lies akthe root of Irish discontent. It is a ques- tion of nationality as truly as in Hungary or in Poland." "Special grievances or anomalies may aggravate, but do not cause it, and they 'become formidable only in as far as they are connected with it." We cannot stifle this nationalism. Past history proves that, and I do not see why any of us should wish to do so. Is not this sentiment'part of the lifeblood of a nation, and are not all civilised people the better for the responsi- bffity o y lift; Conduct, of .their 'own affairs? That, at least, is e (*Striae of thrtfounders of Liberalism: Con- sider t IrnoinfousiXistd of energy caused in Ireland, and, for the matter of that, in England too by this coo- . stout conflict with an alien rule. Consider the frightful rateAtt which the population in parts of the country, 4nd ' ,•as &whole, has diminished.. . ' i • The'densuse4 whiebdal24l were 8.200.000,

" In Belfast there are 80,000 Roman Catholics out of a population of between 250,000 and 300,000, and there are 80 principal officers drawing £18,600 a year. "How many of those offices de you think," says Mr. Gladstone, are held by Roman Catholics in thiseeiberal Protestant city, where they are above religious bigotry—(laughter)— and are the friends of liberty and inequality ? (Re- newed laughter.) Let us see what a splendid example I they set when they came forward with an untruth in their mouths to make this charge against the Roman Catholics. (Cheers.) Well, gentlemen, out of the happy holders and receivers of this £16,600 a year there. are exactly two Roman Catholics—(cries of "Oh ")e- -two—and how much do you think the two get ? Whyse between them they get £3OO a year.. (Laughter.)e There is the liberality of Belfast. (Cheers.) It is go I wonder that they think,that another state of things may be unfavourableperhips• to, that eistreordinaryennooe poly—(laughter and cheers)—and therefore, like other , monopolists, they shout and howl before he time comes I to see if they can infect others with some portion of I their unreasonable alarms, athlete draw therefore into.l, their camp men whose principles and whose traditions must make them their resolietteepponentss" Here I we begin to, have - an - inkling 'of the reasons for the vigorous demonstration, and tall talk of the Orangemen. But I think' It is worth while to look still more closely into presene state of affairs, as accounting- for some of the more violent opposition to Home Rule., and I therefore give-the following extracts trom a most able article in this • month's " Contemporary " by an Irish Preskiy- terian Minister. Both the following tablet, and his , connnents upon it are: I think, well worth attention : I Roman Bpisco- Presby- I • . Catholics. palions. terians . RETURN' OF TIIE WARRINGTON MILITIA. On Saturday the Warrington Militia (3rd Batt Ilion South Lancashire Regiment) returned to Warrington from Altcar, where they luid been in training. They marched from the railway station to the barracks, headed by the band of the regiment, playing lively airs. At the barracks they were dismiss}, and they afterwards exchanged their regimental clothing for their ordinary everyday suit. In the afternoon 1 tilose who reside in Liverpool and elsewhere were marched to the station, and were booked, to their i various destinations.

On Thyrsday morning Adam Tyrer, a lasher-on, aged 18. of Westleigh Mill, was kilted by a fall of roof whilst working at the Abram Colliery. ,
THE LEIGFI ENGINENIES'S STRIKE.

Two new enginemen have been engaged at the Plank lane Collieries Leigh, and two out of the four pits. employing 1,000 men, resumed workyesterday morning The other 1,000 are expected to start on Monday.

NEW Yourt, TnuesiiAy!—lntense heat cc:manned tO prevail on Tuesday throughout the greater pert of the, Unitea States. Numerous deaths have occurred', and many persons have been prostrated:W.-the. larger cities. At Chicago fifty deaths are reported,,whlle over one hundred people,trave t:nen overcdme.by the great heat: The hospitals are filled with patients, and the police facilities are unequal tn the task of removing those suffering from sunstroke. There is also a high death- rate among the horseS used .in, public conveyances in Philadelphia and New York. Storms occurred, how- ever, at many points during Tuesday evening, resulting in a fall of the' temperature, and there are general in- dications that a cool wave is now advancing.

div.head: QUEEN'S LETTER.
div.p: THE QUEEN'S LETTER.

• We have received an etching fac-simile, guinea •edition, of the Queen's letter to the nation ou the .ileath,of the Duke of Clarence. It has been issued in the highest style Of art by Messrs, Raphael Tuck 'end Sons. who are 'generously. devoting the whole of the profits of the publication to the Gordon-Boys' tflonie. A.first instalment of „t6OO has already been forwarded. The symboliC border has been. designed by Mr. E. J. Poynter, 8.A., and it,:is'a most elabor- ate 4nd artistic piece of work.- , Toe'design is composed of an' architectural fram* work with thirteen,allegoric4l figures supporting a panel on which..the-QUHNIFB letter is-displayed. A ;winged figure odeach side at the top is. 'drawing aside a curtain to exhibit the letter. The centre is surmounteu by the Royal Arms with a branch of the Rose-, symbolic of the Royal Family of England twining beside it. The Rose is used as a leading leature.thronghout•the design. On the left ,draped in the flacr,is Britannia accompanied by Grief, repre- sented by a veiled figure, who offers ,a wreath as a tribute of mourning, and pointing towards a harp, lying recumbent at • the base,. with one of the strings snapped asunder, and adjacent to a broken ;branch of the Rose; both symbolic of the untimely death of the Duke of Clarence and Avondale. The pedestal on which britannia stands is supported by two typical Genii, representing her Empire over the •sea. in the centre of the base the Shamrock and Thistle are combined with the Rose, indicative of the united people to whom the, letter is addressed. The •clear, bold handwriting, of the IZtueen is a •conipicuous feature ; and the issue in every way sustains the reputation of the artist-, the etcher, and the publishers. •

div.head: WILL OF THE LATE-. MIL. EDWARD
div.p: WILL OF THE LATE-. MIL. EDWARD
WHITLE)3.

The will of the late Mr. Edward Whitley,.M.P. for the ! Everton Division of the city, was proved on Thursday at the Liverpool Probate Court. The will,, which is a very carefully prepared and voluminous document, is dated the 26th December, lan; and the executors are Messrs. Francis T. Maddock, John Thomas Whitley (nephew), and Joseph Robinson. The gross value of the personal estate of the deceased is given at £447',3.53, and the net value £445,554. anumber of small legacies is bequeathed, and an annuity, of £2Oll is bequeathed to his sister Mary. All the deceased's plate. carriares, pic- tures, valuables, and horsehold. effects are left to his widow for her sole use, ad the pieces of plate presented to Mr. Whitley by the people of Liverpool, the Law Society, and other bodies, he beqpeaths to his wife, with the request that they may be handed down as heirlooms. He gives to the executors above- mentioned. as trustees, the house known as " The- Lawn," at Rhyl, and the " Dola.wert estate adjoining,. upon trust, for the uso and enioyment of his widow du:s- ing her life, and to form part of the residue of the esta.V. Re bequeaths to his trusteea the sum of £150,000 to be invested for his wife.during her life. "knowing that she will maintain and educate their chitdren;up to the age of twenty-one ;" and afterthat the balance to go into the residae of the estate. Be also gives to his trusteea the sum of £30,000 for the benefit a his daughter,. Mary Eleanor Whitley, and her children. The deceased's shares in the firm of Greene!' and Whitley, brewers, Warrington, subject to. certain annuities, the deceased gimes in trust to his sons Edward William, Hebert, and Charles Whitey and their heirs, and the residue of tbe real and personal estate "to the use of my valued friend,, Francis Thornhill Maddock," Joseph Robinson, and John Thomas Whitley, in trust for the deceased's children. The will gives details aud minute instructions to. the trustees as to how the money left by tise deceased shall be invested.

here; I will be back!" and before he could question her further, she was gone. Mrs. Field sat by her window, wondering so sadly, If happiness would ever be hers again, when Cecil came in to her. '"Aunt Mabel," she said, "the woods are lovely. Come out to your resting-place under the pine- tree." And Mrs.. Yield went gladly, for merry Cecil was unusually quiet and thoughtful. At last she said: rC '"Dear. Aunt, Mabel; weal you sing 'Bonnie Charlie 'for me 2" • ' "Oh, child, not that! I have not, sung it since I sung it to my husband eight years ago," sighed Mrs. Field. " Ah, sing it now for me, I beg," pleaded Cecil. And Mrs. Field did sing. Her voice felted sadly, as the bitter memories mingled with the strains of the song, but it gathered strength and sweetness as she sang. So absorbed was she in the thoughts the melody brought back to her, that she did not miss Cecil, who had quietly stolen away; and when she heard a soft footfall behind her, she still sang on; and the plaintive refrain to the old Jacobite song-- "Better lo'ed ye canna be; Will ye no come back again r had never sounded sweeter to the listener's ears. But it was not Cecil. A voioe long unheard sounded in her ears: "Mabel, my wife, forgive me l" and turning, she saw-;--her harband. With a wild shriek she fell fainting at his feet; and Cecil, rushing to her aid, cried: " 0 ! I have killed her!" Just then Mr. Penfield's nephew came back, and seeing Cecil's distress, hastened to her assist- ance. Together they laid the poor lady on the soft, mossy bank, and with water from the brook revived her. Starting up, she cried to Cecil: "Is my husband here, or is it some awful dream 2" "He is indeed here," answered Cecil. "Will you forgive me for letting you meet so abruptly I thought perhaps when you saw him you would be glad. And oh! Aunt Mabel, forgive him I Some- thing so dreadful has happened that he peecls all your love and pity." 'What is it 7" gasped Mrs. Field. And Cecil sadly answered: "Ho is blind I" Then a great wave of tenclereess surged over the wronged wife's heart, and rising, she said to Cecil: "Take me to my husband." "He is here," replied Cecil; for Mr. Penfield had followed the sound of his wife's voice, and now be knelt beside her. "Oh, wife I" he said again, 'forgive me! Let me feel your hand in mine, for I cannot see you—l am blind! God has punished me. I vowed never to loOk on your face again, and Be has taken from me the ;rower to do so." "Charlton," said his wife, tenderly, "I forgave you long ago, and—l love your Then she lifted • his face to hers, and kissed first the sightless eyes; , then, blushing as deeply as any maiden, she t 1 kissed his lips. "So, love," she said, "let the past be buried," She was very happy when, later, 'she went back to her luxurious home with her husband, his nephew, young Charles Penfield (who had been his most devoted attendant since the loss of his eyesight) and Cecil. It seemed a perfect haven of rest after her years of restless wanderings, and /49 I:gbter ituux even in the first days of her Wedded bliss. Her husband was her lover again, dearer, truer and better loved than ever before, "Married lovers," Cecil calls them, and declares, laughingly, that some day she will write their story. But perhaps she will have her own to write first; for the night before Charlie Penfield went back to college, she sang to him: "Better lo'ed ye canna be; Will ye no come back again?" And be promised. A SIGNINCANT MOVEMENT. Our friend Jones (George P.), a genial and accom- modating dentist, sat in his office one day, with several ladies present for whom he had done dental work, engaged in social, friendly chat, when in came a countryman—a stalwart, solid-looking man, clad in homespun—who wanted a tooth pulled. It was "an old grinder, aching dreadfully," and his teeth were "awful hard to get out." The doctor took him into the operating room—a small space simply partitioned off from the main room by curtains—and examined the tooth. It was really a tough looking case. The tooth —an upper molar—was badly decayed, and the jaw inflamed. Jones suggested that he had better take gas. " Gas I what's that ?" George P. explained. " Sho 7 Haow ye talk I An' it 'll send me off so't I won't know noth'n anyhow ?" "Yes, sir—it will render you entirely insensible to pain—insensible to everything—for a short period. But it is not dangerous—not in the least.' "Wal,—go ahead. I 'll take the gas." The doctor brought forward the inhaling tube, and bade the man make ready. "Hold on jest a minnit, Doctor." And thereupon the man dived his hand down into his deep pocket, and drew out a fist full of silver coin and crumpled bank-note. "Never mind that now, my good sir," said Jones. "You can pay me when the tooth is pulled." "Don't you worry, Doctor, I ain't a goin' to pay you now, never fear; but you say as haow that ere gas 'll send me clean off entirely; and I thought 'twould be well to know jest "mow much spondulix I had in my pocket afore I went. You 'll excus me, bnt I 'ye travelled l" A giggle from the outer room told that the scene was enjoyed there;i and George P. fancied, then and there, as it truly proved, that it would be a long time before he would hear the last of that gas patient.
